- **colour.cie1931-2deg-cmf-file** [datum] — CIE 1931 2-degree colour matching functions, CVRL file. The file refs/data/cie1931_2deg_cvrl.csv holds the CIE 1931 2-degree colour matching functions fetched from CVRL (ciexyz31_1.csv): 1 nm step, columns wavelength (nm), xbar, ybar, zbar. Checked by inspection of the file: 471 data rows, no header line, wavelength 360 nm to 830 nm in unit steps, values with 12 decimal places. The README states only the source URL, the 1 nm step and the column order; the wavelength range and row count are properties of the file, not stated in the README.

- **colour.cie1931-2deg-cmf-short-wavelength-error** [result] — CIE 1931 2-deg CMFs are in error at short wavelengths. The README states that the CIE 1924 V(lambda) used to construct the CIE 1931 2-deg CMFs seriously underestimates sensitivity at wavelengths below 460 nm, so that these CMFs are seriously in error at short wavelengths; the Judd and Judd-Vos modifications are attempts to overcome this.  
  `\text{CIE 1931 2-deg CMFs: error for } \lambda<460\ {\rm nm}`  
  src: `data/cie1931_2deg_cvrl_README` Notes paragraph 1 (last sentences); anchor: “at wavelengths below 460 nm, so that these CMFs are seriously in error at short”
- **colour.display-exposure-convention** [pipeline] — Scalar exposure applied before the tone operator (project convention). Project convention: the scaled luminance entering the tone operator is L_sc = t_exp k_exp Y_pre, where Y_pre is the unexposed Y of the rendered spectrum (the Y of pipeline.display-colour before any exposure factor is applied), t_exp the exposure time and k_exp the exposure scale factor. Domain: require finite Y_pre, t_exp, k_exp, L_sc, with Y_pre >= 0, t_exp > 0, k_exp > 0, and [k_exp] = [Y_pre]^-1 s^-1 so that L_sc is dimensionless; any violation raises. A single scalar t_exp k_exp is applied; t_exp, k_exp (or their product) is a logged parameter of every rendered frame. L_sc is the Reinhard scaled luminance, so L_d = L_sc/(1+L_sc) and its inverse L_sc = L_d/(1-L_d) recovers Y_pre = L_sc/(t_exp k_exp).  
  `L_{sc} = t_{exp}\,k_{exp}\,Y_{pre}, \qquad Y_{pre}\ \text{finite},\ Y_{pre}\ge 0,\ t_{exp}>0,\ k_{exp}>0,\ [k_{exp}] = [Y_{pre}]^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}`  
  src: `PRD` The shot, Primary output; anchor: “Display images and video are derived with a stated camera,”
- **colour.k-cd-luminous-efficacy** [constant] — Luminous efficacy K_cd = 683 lm/W at 540e12 Hz (SI definition). The SI defining constant K_cd, the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 x 10^12 Hz, is 683 lm/W (exact). It defines the candela: 1 lm/W = 1 cd sr/W. Converts radiant power to luminous flux at that single frequency; the brochure gives no photopic efficiency function, so it does not by itself convert broadband spectral radiance to luminance.  
  `K_{cd}=683\ \mathrm{lm\,W^{-1}}\quad(\nu=540\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{Hz})`  
  src: `bipm_2019_si_brochure` Sec. 2.2 (Table 1, defining constants) and Sec. 2.3.1 (the candela); anchor: “radiation of frequency 540 × 1012 Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit ”

- **colour.reinhard-bounded-output** [result] — Eq. 3 output bounded to the displayable range. The simple operator is guaranteed to bring all luminances within a displayable range (for L >= 0, L_d = L/(1+L) lies in [0,1)); high luminances are scaled by approximately 1/L and low luminances by 1.  
  `L \ge 0 \Rightarrow 0 \le L_d < 1`  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` p. 4, after eq. 3; anchor: “Note that high luminances are scaled by approximately 1/L, while”
- **colour.reinhard-dynamic-range-definition** [definition] — Dynamic range of a scene (computer graphics). In computer graphics the dynamic range of a scene is expressed as the ratio of the highest scene luminance to the lowest scene luminance; photographers instead use the ratio of the highest and lowest luminance regions where detail is visible, expressed in zones (differences of log scene luminance).  
  `\mathrm{DR} = L_{\max} / L_{\min}`  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` p. 3, section 2 (Dynamic range); anchor: “scene is expressed as the ratio of the highest scene luminance”
- **colour.reinhard-global-limitation** [approximation] — Global operator loses detail at very high dynamic range. For many high-dynamic-range images the compression of the global operators (eq. 3, eq. 4) preserves detail in low-contrast areas, but for very high dynamic range images important detail is still lost; the authors then use a local dodging-and-burning operator.  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` p. 4, after eq. 4; anchor: “dynamic range images important detail is still lost.”
- **colour.reinhard-key-default** [constant] — Default key value a = 0.18. For normal-key scenes, the authors choose a = 0.18 in eq. 2 to target middle-grey, before tone compression.  
  `a = 0.18`  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` p. 4, before eq. 2; anchor: “of the displayed image, or 0.18 on a scale from zero to one.”
- **colour.reinhard-key-value-definition** [definition] — Key value. The value of the parameter a in eq. 2 is called the key value, because it relates to the key of the image after applying the scaling.  
  `\text{key value} \equiv a`  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` p. 4, after eq. 2; anchor: “of parameter a the “key value”, because it relates to the key of the”
- **colour.reinhard-log-average-as-key** [approximation] — Log-average luminance as scene key. The log-average luminance of the scene is taken as a useful approximation to the subjective key of the scene; eq. 2 scales the estimated scene key to a before tone compression (middle-grey 0.18 for normal-key scenes); for low-key or high-key images the user chooses a different a.  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` p. 4, section 3.1; anchor: “view the log-average luminance as a useful approximation to the”
- **colour.reinhard-log-average-luminance** [equation] — Log-average (world) luminance, Reinhard eq. 1. Reinhard et al. define the log-average luminance of the scene, used as an approximation to the scene key, from the world luminance L_w(x,y) of all N pixels with a small offset delta that avoids the singularity at black pixels. AS PRINTED in this tech report (p. 4 page image) the prefactor 1/N stands outside the exponential, i.e. (1/N) exp(sum log(delta+L_w)), which is not the geometric mean described by the prose name 'log-average'; the form exp((1/N) sum log(delta+L_w)) would be the geometric mean. Record the printed form and flag it; the reboot must not silently pick one.  
  `\bar{L}_w = \frac{1}{N}\exp\left(\sum_{x,y}\log\left(\delta + L_w(x,y)\right)\right)`  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` eq. 1 (p. 4); anchor: “view the log-average luminance as a useful approximation to the”
- **colour.reinhard-scaled-luminance** [equation] — Scaled luminance with key value a, Reinhard eq. 2. The world luminance is linearly scaled so that the log-average luminance maps to the key value a (default middle-grey 0.18), giving the scaled luminance L(x,y) that is the input of the tone-mapping operators.  
  `L(x,y) = \frac{a}{\bar{L}_w} L_w(x,y)`  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` eq. 2 (p. 4); anchor: “where L(x, y) is a scaled luminance and a = 0.18.”
- **colour.reinhard-simple-inverse** [equation] — Inverse of the Reinhard simple operator. The inverse of the simple global operator L_d = L_sc/(1+L_sc) (Reinhard eq. 3) is L_sc = L_d/(1-L_d). It is valid only for 0 <= L_d < 1; L_d >= 1 has no preimage (the operator maps [0, inf) onto [0, 1)), and L_d -> 1 diverges, so code must raise on L_d >= 1 or L_d < 0 and never clamp.  
  `L_{sc} = \frac{L_d}{1 - L_d}, \qquad 0 \le L_d < 1`  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` eq. 3 (p. 4), inverted; anchor: “tone mapping operator with these characteristics is given by:”
- **colour.reinhard-simple-operator** [equation] — Simple global tone-mapping operator, Reinhard eq. 3. The simple global operator maps the scaled luminance L to display luminance Ld = L/(1+L): high luminances are compressed by about 1/L, low luminances are left scaled by 1.  
  `L_d(x,y) = \frac{L(x,y)}{1 + L(x,y)}`  
  src: `reinhard_2002_tonemapping` eq. 3 (p. 4); anchor: “tone mapping operator with these characteristics is given by:”

## eos

- **eos.electron-pressure-magnetised** [equation] — Pressure of the ideal magnetised degenerate electron gas. Electron pressure of a magnetised Fermi gas expressed through the chemical potential mu and temperature T, as a sum over Landau levels n = 0..n_max of Fermi-Dirac integrals I_{1/2}(chi_n, tau_n); P_r and T_r are the relativistic units of pressure and temperature.  
  `P_e = P_r \frac{b\,\tau_0^{3/2}}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi^2}\sum_{n=0}^{n_{\max}} (2 - \delta_{n0})(1 + 2bn)^{1/4} I_{1/2}(\chi_n, \tau_n)`  
  src: `potekhin_yakovlev_2001_cooling` eq. 12, p. 4; anchor: “pressure can be expressed through the chemical potential”
- **eos.notation-electron-gas** [notation] — Magnetised degenerate-electron-gas symbols. Symbols used for the ideal magnetised electron gas pressure: relativistic field strength, cyclotron frequency, Compton wavelength, Landau-level index, chemical potential, and relativistic pressure and temperature units.  
  src: `potekhin_yakovlev_2001_cooling` p. 1 (b, lambda_e, omega_c) and p. 4, eq. 12 and text; anchor: “b = h̄ωc /me c2 = B12 /44.14 is the magnetic field strength”
- **eos.relativistic-units-pr-tr** [constant] — Relativistic units of pressure and temperature. Relativistic unit of pressure P_r = m_e c^2/lambda_e^3 = 1.4218e25 dyn cm^-2 and of temperature T_r = m_e c^2/k_B = 5.930e9 K, used to reduce the electron-gas variables.  
  `P_r = m_e c^2/\lambda_e^3 \approx 1.4218\times 10^{25}\ \mathrm{dyn\,cm^{-2}}, \qquad T_r = m_e c^2/k_B \approx 5.930\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{K}`  
  src: `potekhin_yakovlev_2001_cooling` p. 4, text after eq. 12; anchor: “Pr = me c2 /λ3e ≈ 1.4218 × 1025 dyn cm−2 and Tr =”
- **eos.surface-gravity** [equation] — Surface gravity with the GR factor. Near the surface (z much less than R) the general-relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium reduces to the Newtonian form dP/dz = g rho, with surface gravity g = GM/(R^2 sqrt(1 - r_g/R)); z is local proper depth, increasing inward.  
  `dP/dz = g\rho, \qquad g = GM/\left(R^2 \sqrt{1 - r_g/R}\right)`  
  src: `potekhin_yakovlev_2001_cooling` p. 3 (text after eq. 7 introduction, before eq. 7); anchor: “dP/dz = gρ, where g = GM/(R2 1 − rg /R ) is the sur-”
- **eos.thin-envelope-newtonian-hydrostatics** [approximation] — Thin-envelope plane-parallel Newtonian hydrostatics. For depths z much smaller than R the GR hydrostatic equilibrium is replaced by dP/dz = g rho with constant surface gravity g; in the heat-blanketing envelope one neglects the variation of gravitational acceleration; one neglects neutrino-induced flux variation only when those losses are small, and lateral Ts variation when its length scale greatly exceeds z_b.  
  src: `potekhin_pons_page_2015_thermal` Sect. 5.1, pp. 38–39, before eq. 38; anchor: “can neglect the variation of the gravitational acceleration in this layer”

## gr

- **gr.apparent-quantities** [equation] — Redshifted (apparent) stellar quantities. Apparent quantities detected by a distant observer, from local-frame quantities: R_infty = R/sqrt(1 - r_g/R), T_eff^infty = T_eff sqrt(1 - r_g/R), L_ph^infty = (1 - r_g/R) L_ph (the source cites Thorne 1977).  
  `R_\infty=\frac{R}{\sqrt{1-r_g/R}},\qquad T^\infty_{\rm eff}=T_{\rm eff}\sqrt{1-r_g/R},\qquad L^\infty_{\rm ph}=\left(1-\frac{r_g}{R}\right)L_{\rm ph}`  
  src: `potekhin_pons_page_2015_thermal` Sect. 5, eq. 40; anchor: “(“apparent”) quantities as detected by a distant observer are (Thorne 1977):”
- **gr.approx-opaque-surface** [approximation] — Opaque star with transparent exterior. The region r < R is totally opaque and, apart from beaming conditions at the emitting surface, the region r > R is totally transparent: effects on photon propagation other than gravity are ignored. Null geodesics do not depend on photon frequency.  
  src: `pechenick_1983_gr_ray_tracing` Sect. II, pp. 846-847; anchor: “We also assume that the region r<R is totally”
- **gr.approx-schwarzschild-exterior** [approximation] — Static Schwarzschild exterior for a slowly rotating star. The brightness of the rotating star is taken to be its instantaneous value if the star were stationary; the Kerr metric and frame dragging are not used and the exterior is Schwarzschild with mass M.  
  src: `pechenick_1983_gr_ray_tracing` Sect. II, p. 846; anchor: “not use the Kerr metric and we neglect the”
- **gr.beloborodov-cosine-error-bound** [datum] — Accuracy of the cosine relation. Maximum fractional error e = delta(beta)/beta of the bending angle beta = psi - alpha from the cosine relation for R = 3 r_g is 3 percent (at alpha = 90 deg), and e < 1 percent for alpha < 75 deg. High accuracy is maintained for R > 2 r_g (error map in the source Fig. 2).  
  src: `beloborodov_2002_ray_tracing` Sect. 2, text below eq. 1; Fig. 2; anchor: “ror is emax = 3% (at α = 90o ) and e < 1% for α < 75o”
- **gr.beloborodov-cosine-relation** [approximation] — Beloborodov light-bending cosine relation. Approximate relation between the emission angle alpha at radius R and the polar angle psi of the emission point seen from infinity for a Schwarzschild star: 1 - cos alpha = (1 - cos psi)(1 - r_g/R). It replaces the exact elliptic-integral relation (gr.bending-integral with gr.emission-angle-impact-parameter).  
  `1-\cos\alpha=(1-\cos\psi)\left(1-\frac{r_g}{R}\right)`  
  src: `beloborodov_2002_ray_tracing` eq. 1 (abstract and Sect. 2); anchor: “1 − cos α = (1 − cos ψ)(1 − rg /R) where R/rg is the emission”
- **gr.bending-integral** [equation] — Exact bending integral psi(b), Schwarzschild. Polar angle psi (measured from the escape direction) of a photon at radius R with impact parameter b, in terms of its escape trajectory: psi = int_R^infty (-u^psi/u^r) dr = int_R^infty (dr/r^2) [1/b^2 - (1/r^2)(1 - r_g/r)]^(-1/2).  
  `\psi=\int_R^\infty\frac{-u^\psi}{u^r}\,dr=\int_R^\infty\frac{dr}{r^2}\left[\frac{1}{b^2}-\frac{1}{r^2}\left(1-\frac{r_g}{r}\right)\right]^{-1/2}`  
  src: `beloborodov_2002_ray_tracing` Appendix, eq. 9; anchor: “escape direction. Then at radius R the photon has”
- **gr.bending-integral-finite-radius** [equation] — Bending integral from a finite camera radius r_cam. Finite swept polar angle psi_cam of a photon with impact parameter b between the stellar surface r = R and a camera at a finite Schwarzschild radius r_cam > R. psi_cam is distinct from the existing infinity-referenced psi of gr.bending-integral (Bel02 eq. 9, psi = 0 at infinity), to which it tends as r_cam -> infinity. It is Beloborodov eq. 9 with the upper limit infinity replaced by r_cam, equivalently Pechenick eq. 2.12 with its lower limit u = 0 replaced by u = M/r_cam: psi_cam = int_R^{r_cam} K_b(r) dr with K_b(r) = b/[r^2 sqrt(1 - b^2 (1 - r_g/r)/r^2)], which equals the printed (1/r^2)[1/b^2 - (1/r^2)(1 - r_g/r)]^(-1/2) for b > 0 and includes the radial ray b = 0 (K_b = 0, psi_cam = 0) without division by zero. In u = M/r (geometric M): psi_cam = int_{M/r_cam}^{M/R} (b/M)[1 - (b/M)^2 (1 - 2u)u^2]^(-1/2) du, equal to Pechenick's [u_b^2 - (1 - 2u)u^2]^(-1/2), u_b = M/b, for b > 0. This holds when the ray has no radial turning point in (R, r_cam], i.e. it arrives at the camera outgoing with 0 <= b <= b_max = R (1 - r_g/R)^(-1/2) (for R > 3GM/c^2). The grazing hit b = b_max is included: its turning point is at r = R itself, where K_b has an integrable 1/sqrt(r - R) endpoint singularity. A ray that arrives outgoing with b > b_max came from the sky through a periastron r_tp < r_cam, the largest root of r^3 - b^2 r + b^2 r_g = 0, and psi_cam = int_{r_tp}^{r_cam} K_b dr + int_{r_tp}^{infinity} K_b dr. A ray that arrives ingoing came from the sky with psi_cam = int_{r_cam}^{infinity} K_b dr. psi_cam may exceed pi (multiple images). For r_cam -> infinity the hit case reduces to Beloborodov eq. 9 and Pechenick eq. 2.12. b is a constant of the geodesic, so these integrals are the same for any camera velocity; only the map from pixel to (b, arrival branch) depends on the camera frame.

- **gr.camera-aberration** [equation] — Relativistic aberration between camera and static (FIDO) frames. A camera moves with speed beta relative to the local FIDO (the static observer when a = 0) along its own Cartesian basis vector e_y = B. e_x is perpendicular to e_y and lies in the plane of e_r-hat and e_phi-hat, and e_z completes a right-handed set. A point (theta_cs, phi_cs) on the camera's local sky defines the unit vector N = (sin theta_cs cos phi_cs, sin theta_cs sin phi_cs, cos theta_cs), which points in the direction of the incoming ray. The ray's direction of motion n_F measured by the FIDO, in Cartesian axes aligned with the camera's, is n_F,y = (-N_y + beta)/(1 - beta N_y), n_F,x = -sqrt(1 - beta^2) N_x/(1 - beta N_y), n_F,z = -sqrt(1 - beta^2) N_z/(1 - beta N_y).

N is the camera-sky direction of the incoming ray. b is the ray's axial angular momentum, with p_t = -1. alpha and omega are evaluated at the camera.

- **gr.camera-four-velocity-static-frame** [equation] — Four-velocity from speed and direction in a local tetrad. Relative to a local tetrad e_(i), a timelike direction is identified with the four-velocity u = c gamma (e_(0) + beta n), with n = sin chi cos xi e_(1) + sin chi sin xi e_(2) + cos chi e_(3) a unit spatial vector, beta the speed in units of c measured by the observer e_(0), and gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - beta^2); then <u, u> = c^2 gamma^2 (-1 + beta^2) = -c^2 for signature +2. Applied to the static tetrad at the camera position (gr.static-tetrad), this gives the camera four-velocity from its speed beta and direction of motion n measured by the local static observer.  
  `\mathbf{u}=c\gamma\left(\mathbf{e}_0+\beta\mathbf{n}\right),\qquad \mathbf{u}^2=\left<\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}\right>_{\mathbf{g}}=c^2\gamma^2\left(-1+\beta^2\right)=-c^2,\quad \mathrm{sign}(\mathbf{g})=+2`

- **gr.camera-projection-convention** [pipeline] — Camera projection: pixel to camera-sky direction (pinhole or equidistant). Project convention for mapping a pixel to a direction on the camera's local sky, in the rest frame of the camera tetrad e_(a)^cam (gr.static-tetrad boosted by gr.tetrad-lorentz-transformation to u_cam). The optical axis is the unit vector a_cam. Image-right u_x and image-up u_y complete an orthonormal triad with u_x x u_y = -a_cam, so the image is unmirrored when viewed looking along a_cam. A pixel at (x_pix, y_pix) has offsets (dx, dy) from the optical-axis pixel (x_pix,0, y_pix,0), with dy positive toward image-up. Its image radius is r_pix = (dx^2 + dy^2)^(1/2) and its azimuth phi_field = atan2(dy, dx). The field angle from the optical axis is theta_field = arctan(r_pix/f_cam) for a pinhole (rectilinear) camera, valid for theta_field < pi/2, or theta_field = r_pix/f_cam for an equidistant fisheye. The focal length f_cam is in pixels and must satisfy f_cam > 0. The field angle is restricted to 0 <= theta_field <= pi (pinhole: 0 <= theta_field < pi/2); the full field of view of the image, rather than theta_field, may exceed pi. On the optical axis (r_pix = 0, theta_field = 0) N_cam(0) = a_cam. The pixel's sky direction is N_cam = cos theta_field a_cam + sin theta_field (cos phi_field u_x + sin phi_field u_y). It points toward the apparent source of the incoming ray, as N in James et al. 2015 eq. A.8. The photon propagates along -N_cam, with p = (h nu_cam/c)(e_(0)^cam - N^a e_(a)^cam), i.e. p^(0) = h nu_cam/c and h nu_cam = c p^(0) = -p_mu u^mu_cam (gr.frequency-ratio-general, gr.tetrad-vector-components).

Here psi is the total swept angle of that image's ray and may exceed pi. Each image contributes separately, and the element's observed flux is the sum over its images. On the primary branch (psi < pi, psi increasing with alpha), d cos alpha/d mu > 0 and the absolute value may be dropped, which gives Beloborodov's printed second equality of eq. 11. On intervals (2n+1)pi < psi < (2n+2)pi (n = 0, 1, ...), d cos alpha/d mu < 0, and the printed signed form gives a negative flux; on 2n pi < psi < (2n+1)pi it is positive. - **gr.photon-sphere** [result] — Photon sphere and the b <= b_max condition. The photon-orbit potential B^-2(r) = (1-2M/r)/r^2 has its maximum at r = 3M (i.e. r = 1.5 r_g) and decreases outside. A photon at r must satisfy b^-2 - B^-2(r) >= 0. For a star with R > 3M a photon emitted from the surface and reaching the observer therefore has b <= b_max (see gr.impact-parameter-max).  
  `B^{-2}(r)=\frac{1-2M/r}{r^2},\qquad b^{-2}-B^{-2}(r)\ge 0,\qquad B^{-2}\ \text{maximal at}\ r=3M`  
  src: `pechenick_1983_gr_ray_tracing` eqs. 2.8-2.10, p. 847; anchor: “has a maximum at r = 3M and”
- **gr.schwarzschild-line-element** [equation] — Schwarzschild line element (a = 0 reduction), exterior metric. Setting a = 0 in the Boyer-Lindquist Kerr line element gives the Schwarzschild line element ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^(-1) dr^2 + r^2 (dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2) in geometrized units G = c = 1 with the mass restored (M here is the length GM/c^2), signature (-,+,+,+). In the project's Gaussian CGS units (t in s, r in cm): ds^2 = -(1 - r_g/r) c^2 dt^2 + (1 - r_g/r)^(-1) dr^2 + r^2 (dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2), with r_g = 2GM/c^2 (dictionary symbol r_g), so g_rr = (1 - r_g/r)^(-1). Applied to a star it describes the exterior r >= R with M the star's gravitational mass, which is the blessed assumption gr.approx-schwarzschild-exterior (Pechenick Sect. II). In the Phi/Lambda convention of gr.notation-potekhin (g_tt = -e^(2 Phi) c^2, g_rr = e^(2 Lambda)) the exterior has e^(2 Phi) = 1 - r_g/r and e^(-2 Lambda) = 1 - r_g/r; the latter corrects the PPP15 eq. 1 misprint e^(2 Lambda) = 1 - 2GM_r/(c^2 r) for r >= R.  
  `ds^2 = -\left(1-\frac{2M}{r}\right)dt^2 + \left(1-\frac{2M}{r}\right)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2\left(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right)\ (G=c=1);\qquad ds^2 = -\left(1-\frac{r_g}{r}\right)c^2dt^2 + \left(1-\frac{r_g}{r}\right)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2\left(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right),\quad r_g = \frac{2GM}{c^2}`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eqs. 1-3 at a = 0, p. 2; anchor: “where $a$ is the angular momentum of the black hole and we use units with $G=c=M”
- **gr.schwarzschild-radius** [definition] — Schwarzschild radius r_g. The Schwarzschild radius of a star of gravitating mass M is r_g = 2GM/c^2; numerically 2.95 km (M/M_sun). Beloborodov (2002) states the same definition.  
  `r_g = \frac{2GM}{c^2}`  
  src: `potekhin_pons_page_2015_thermal` Sect. 2.1, text after eq. 2, p. 5; anchor: “is the Schwarzschild radius, M ≡ MR is the stellar mass,”
- **gr.static-observer-four-velocity** [equation] — Four-velocity of a static observer. The four-velocity of a stationary observer in the Schwarzschild metric is u^mu = [(1-2M/r)^(-1/2), 0, 0, 0] in coordinates (t, r, theta, phi). Geometric units G = c = 1.  
  `u^\mu=\left[(1-2M/r)^{-1/2},0,0,0\right]`

- **gr.static-tetrad** [equation] — Static orthonormal tetrad in Schwarzschild coordinates. In Schwarzschild coordinates (t, r, theta, phi), with metric ds^2 = -(1 - r_s/r) c^2 dt^2 + dr^2/(1 - r_s/r) + r^2 (dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2) and Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c^2, the local tetrad of the static observer is e_(t) = [c (1 - r_s/r)^(1/2)]^(-1) d/dt, e_(r) = (1 - r_s/r)^(1/2) d/dr, e_(theta) = r^(-1) d/dtheta, e_(phi) = (r sin theta)^(-1) d/dphi. The dual tetrad is theta^(t) = c (1 - r_s/r)^(1/2) dt, theta^(r) = dr/(1 - r_s/r)^(1/2), theta^(theta) = r dtheta, theta^(phi) = r sin theta dphi.  
  `\mathbf{e}_{(t)}=\frac{1}{c\sqrt{1-r_s/r}}\partial_t,\qquad \mathbf{e}_{(r)}=\sqrt{1-\frac{r_s}{r}}\,\partial_r,\qquad \mathbf{e}_{(\vartheta)}=\frac{1}{r}\partial_\vartheta,\qquad \mathbf{e}_{(\varphi)}=\frac{1}{r\sin\vartheta}\partial_\varphi`  
  src: `muller_grave_2009_spacetimes` Sect. 2.2.1, eq. 2.2.6 (metric eq. 2.2.1, dual tetrad eq. 2.2.7), PDF p. 22 (printed p. 18); anchor: “In Schwarzschild coordinates $\left\{t\in\setR,r\in\setR^{+},\vartheta\in(0,\pi)”
- **gr.static-tetrad-field-projection** [equation] — Field tensor on the static Schwarzschild tetrad (Wasserman & Shapiro). For a static, axisymmetric, purely magnetic field in a Schwarzschild background (only A_phi nonzero; geometrized units G = c = 1; x = r/2M), Wasserman & Shapiro project the field tensor F_{mu nu} onto a local orthonormal tetrad and obtain F_{phi-hat r-hat} = (1 - x^-1)^(1/2) F_{phi r}/(r sin theta) = B^{theta-hat} and F_{phi-hat theta-hat} = F_{phi theta}/(r^2 sin theta) = -B^{r-hat}, the locally measured field components.  
  `F_{\hat\phi\hat r}=\frac{(1-x^{-1})^{1/2}F_{\phi r}}{r\sin\theta}=B^{\hat\theta},\qquad F_{\hat\phi\hat\theta}=\frac{F_{\phi\theta}}{r^2\sin\theta}=-B^{\hat r},\qquad x\equiv r/2M`

- **gr.tetrad-lorentz-transformation** [equation] — Lorentz transformation of a local tetrad (boost). Any other local tetrad is obtained from a local tetrad e_(k) by e-hat_(i) = A_i^k e_(k), with A an element of the Lorentz group O(1,3): A^T eta A = eta and (det A)^2 = 1. The source prints the Lorentz transformation in the direction of the unit vector n^a, with gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - beta^2), as Lambda_0^0 = gamma, Lambda_a^0 = -beta gamma n_a, Lambda_0^a = -beta gamma n^a, Lambda_b^a = (gamma - 1) n^a n_b + delta^a_b. Used as A, the printed matrix gives e-hat_(0) = gamma (e_(0) - beta n^a e_(a)), the frame of an observer moving with 3-velocity -beta n relative to e_(0). The tetrad of a camera moving with +beta n, whose time leg is u/c = gamma (e_(0) + beta n) (gr.camera-four-velocity-static-frame), uses the same matrix with beta -> -beta, which is the inverse of the printed one: e_(0)^cam = gamma (e_(0) + beta n^a e_(a)), e_(a)^cam = beta gamma n_a e_(0) + [(gamma - 1) n_a n^b + delta_a^b] e_(b).  
  `\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{(i)}=A_i^k\mathbf{e}_{(k)},\qquad \Lambda_0^0=\gamma,\quad \Lambda_a^0=-\beta\gamma n_a,\quad \Lambda_0^a=-\beta\gamma n^a,\quad \Lambda_b^a=(\gamma-1)n^an_b+\delta^a_b,\qquad \gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}`

- **gr.tetrad-vector-components** [equation] — Local (tetrad) and coordinate components of a direction. A null or timelike direction with respect to a local tetrad e_(i) is upsilon = upsilon^(0) e_(0) + psi n, with n = sin chi cos xi e_(1) + sin chi sin xi e_(2) + cos chi e_(3); for a null direction psi = 1 and upsilon^(0) = +-1, the sign giving the time direction. Local components upsilon^(i) and coordinate components upsilon^mu are related by upsilon^mu = upsilon^(i) e_(i)^mu and upsilon^(i) = theta^(i)_mu upsilon^mu, where the dual tetrad satisfies theta^(i)_mu e_(j)^mu = delta^(i)_(j) and theta^(b)_mu = eta^(a)(b) e_(a)mu.  
  `\boldsymbol{\upsilon}=\upsilon^{(0)}\mathbf{e}_{(0)}+\psi\left(\sin\chi\cos\xi\,\mathbf{e}_{(1)}+\sin\chi\sin\xi\,\mathbf{e}_{(2)}+\cos\chi\,\mathbf{e}_{(3)}\right),\qquad \upsilon^{\mu}=\upsilon^{(i)}e_{(i)}^{\mu},\qquad \upsilon^{(i)}=\theta^{(i)}_{\mu}\upsilon^{\mu},\qquad \theta_{\mu}^{(b)}=\eta^{(a)(b)}e_{(a)\mu}`  
  src: `muller_grave_2009_spacetimes` Sect. 1.4, eqs. 1.4.1, 1.4.5b, 1.4.17, 1.4.19, PDF pp. 7-9 (printed pp. 3-5); anchor: “The transformations between a local direction $\upsilon^{(i)}$ and its coordinat”
- **gr.timelike-angular-momentum-from-periastron** [equation] — Specific angular momentum from periastron and energy. Given a chosen periastron r_p and specific energy E of a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic, R(r_p) = 0 fixes the specific angular momentum: L^2 = r_p^2 [E^2/(1 - 2M/r_p) - 1] = r_p^2 [(E^2 - 1) r_p + 2M]/(r_p - 2M) (G = c = 1). In CGS: L^2 = c^2 r_p^2 [E^2/(1 - r_g/r_p) - 1], with L in cm^2 s^-1. L is real for E >= 1 and r_p > 2M. The result is a valid periastron only if r_p is then the largest root of R and dR/dr(r_p) > 0 (gr.timelike-periastron-cubic); otherwise the orbit turns at a larger radius.  
  `L_z^2 = r_p^2\left[\frac{E^2}{1-2M/r_p}-1\right] = \frac{r_p^2\left[(E^2-1)\,r_p+2M\right]}{r_p-2M}`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eq. 6 at a = 0, delta_1 = 1, Q = 0 (solved for L_z), p. 2; anchor: “&\Delta&[\mathcal{Q}+(L_z-aE)^2+\delta_1 r^2]\\”
- **gr.timelike-constants-schwarzschild** [result] — Timelike Schwarzschild geodesic: E, L per unit rest mass; affine parameter is proper time. For a timelike geodesic (delta_1 = 1) at a = 0, take the orbit plane as theta = pi/2, so the Carter constant Q = 0 and |L_z| is the magnitude of the total angular momentum; L_z is signed, and L below is a signed synonym of L_z only because the equatorial plane has been chosen. Dexter & Agol eqs. 5 and 8-10 at a = 0 give the tangent dx^mu/dlambda = (E (1 - 2M/r)^(-1), dr/dlambda, 0, L/r^2) with (dr/dlambda)^2 = E^2 - (1 - 2M/r)(1 + L^2/r^2). Its norm in the a = 0 metric is g_{mu nu} (dx^mu/dlambda)(dx^nu/dlambda) = -delta_1 = -1. So, after choosing the orientation (lambda increasing to the future, E > 0), lambda = tau + C with tau the proper time of the worldline (dtau^2 = -ds^2) and C an additive constant, and dx^mu/dtau = u^mu is the unit four-velocity. Mueller & Grave (2009) state the replacement of the affine parameter by proper time for timelike geodesics. The constants are its covariant components E = -u_t = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dtau and L = u_phi = r^2 dphi/dtau, i.e. energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass. These are the normalised constants of DA09 Sect. 2, whose equations carry no rest mass m; DA09 Sect. 3 instead defines gamma = E/m with an explicit m, and the two agree only when the Sect. 2 E is read per unit rest mass (m = 1). Geometric units G = c = 1. In CGS, with t and tau in s: E = (1 - r_g/r) dt/dtau is dimensionless, the conserved energy divided by the rest energy m c^2, and L = r^2 dphi/dtau (cm^2 s^-1) is the angular momentum per unit rest mass.  
  `E = -u_t = \left(1-\frac{2M}{r}\right)\frac{dt}{d\tau},\qquad L_z = u_\phi = r^2\frac{d\phi}{d\tau},\qquad g_{\mu\nu}\frac{dx^\mu}{d\lambda}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\lambda} = -\delta_1 = -1\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda = \tau + C\qquad (a=0,\ \theta=\pi/2,\ \mathcal{Q}=0,\ G=c=1)`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eqs. 5-10 at a = 0, delta_1 = 1, p. 2; anchor: “and the constants of the motion are the angular momentum about the black hole sp”
- **gr.timelike-dphi-dtau-schwarzschild** [equation] — dphi/dtau on a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic. On a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic in the plane theta = pi/2 with specific angular momentum L (per unit rest mass), the azimuth advances as dphi/dtau = L/r^2 (geometric units). This follows from Dexter & Agol eq. 9 at a = 0, with eqs. 5 and 10. In CGS: dphi/dtau = L/r^2, with L in cm^2 s^-1 and tau in s. The sign of L fixes the sense of rotation and is a free choice of orientation.  
  `\frac{d\phi}{d\tau} = \frac{L_z}{r^2}\qquad (a=0,\ \theta=\pi/2,\ \delta_1=1)`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eq. 9 with eqs. 5 and 10 at a = 0, p. 2; anchor: “\int^r \frac{dr}{\sqrt{R}} = \int^\theta \frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{\Theta}},”
- **gr.timelike-dt-dtau-schwarzschild** [equation] — dt/dtau on a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic. On a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic with specific energy E (per unit rest mass), the coordinate time advances with proper time as dt/dtau = E (1 - 2M/r)^(-1) (geometric units). This follows from Dexter & Agol eq. 8 at a = 0 together with eq. 10. In CGS, with t and tau in s: dt/dtau = E (1 - r_g/r)^(-1).  
  `\frac{dt}{d\tau} = \frac{E}{1-2M/r}\qquad (a=0,\ \delta_1=1,\ G=c=1)`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eq. 8 with eq. 10 at a = 0, delta_1 = 1, p. 2; anchor: “The equations of motion for the cyclic coordinates are”
- **gr.timelike-periastron-cubic** [equation] — Periastron condition R(r_p) = 0 as a cubic. A radial turning point r_p of a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic (a = 0, delta_1 = 1, Q = 0) is a root of R(r_p) = 0, i.e. dr/dtau = 0. Dividing by r_p > 0 gives the cubic (E^2 - 1) r_p^3 + 2M r_p^2 - L^2 r_p + 2M L^2 = 0 (G = c = 1). In CGS: (E^2 - 1) r_p^3 + r_g r_p^2 - (L^2/c^2) r_p + r_g L^2/c^2 = 0. For an incoming orbit from infinity with E >= 1, the periastron is the largest real root; the rule is not claimed for E < 1. It is a true minimum of r only if it is a simple root with dR/dr(r_p) > 0, since d^2r/dtau^2 = (1/2) d(R/r^4)/dr. A double root can support a circular orbit or asymptotic approach to it; it is not a finite-time simple turning point.  
  `(E^2-1)\,r_p^3 + 2M\,r_p^2 - L_z^2\,r_p + 2M\,L_z^2 = 0`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eq. 6 at a = 0, delta_1 = 1, Q = 0, p. 2; anchor: “&\Delta&[\mathcal{Q}+(L_z-aE)^2+\delta_1 r^2]\\”
- **gr.timelike-proper-time-quadrature** [equation] — Proper-time quadrature along a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic. Proper time along a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic (a = 0, delta_1 = 1, equatorial) follows from Dexter & Agol eq. 10 at a = 0, lambda = int r^2 dr/sqrt(R), with lambda = tau + C (gr.timelike-constants-schwarzschild). Elapsed proper time is the unsigned integral dtau = |dr|/sqrt(E^2 - (1 - 2M/r)(1 + L^2/r^2)) > 0, whichever way r moves, so it is positive on the inbound leg as well. For an orbit that comes in from r_1, passes its periastron r_p (an accessible simple root of R) and goes out to r_2, the elapsed proper time is the two-leg sum Delta tau = int_{r_p}^{r_1} dr/sqrt(...) + int_{r_p}^{r_2} dr/sqrt(...), each leg integrated with increasing r. The two-leg rule is derived here from eq. 10; DA09 print a turning-point sum only for null geodesics (Sect. 3), not as a timelike result. The integrand has an integrable 1/sqrt(r - r_p) singularity at r_p. The worldline x^mu(tau) then follows from t(tau) = int E (1 - 2M/r)^(-1) dtau and phi(tau) = int (L/r^2) dtau. In CGS: dtau = |dr|/sqrt(c^2 E^2 - (1 - r_g/r)(c^2 + L^2/r^2)), tau in s.  
  `d\tau = \frac{r^2\,\lvert dr\rvert}{\sqrt{R(r)}} = \frac{\lvert dr\rvert}{\sqrt{E^2-(1-2M/r)(1+L_z^2/r^2)}};\qquad \Delta\tau_{r_1\to r_p\to r_2} = \left(\int_{r_p}^{r_1}+\int_{r_p}^{r_2}\right)\frac{dr}{\sqrt{E^2-(1-2M/r)(1+L_z^2/r^2)}}`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eq. 10 at a = 0, delta_1 = 1 (derivation, p. 2); Sect. 3 turning-point rule for null geodesics (text before eq. 20, p. 3), quoted as the structural analogue only; anchor: “Upon encountering a turning point, the sign of $u$ is reversed, so that the tota”
- **gr.timelike-radial-equation-schwarzschild** [equation] — Radial equation of a timelike Schwarzschild geodesic. For a timelike geodesic in Schwarzschild (a = 0, delta_1 = 1, equatorial, Q = 0), Dexter & Agol's radial function (eq. 6) reduces to R(r) = r^4 E^2 - (r^2 - 2Mr)(L^2 + r^2). With dr/dtau = ±sqrt(R)/r^2 (eq. 10 at a = 0, lambda = tau) this is (dr/dtau)^2 = E^2 - (1 - 2M/r)(1 + L^2/r^2). Units are geometric (G = c = 1), with E and L per unit rest mass (gr.timelike-constants-schwarzschild). In CGS: (dr/dtau)^2 = c^2 E^2 - (1 - r_g/r)(c^2 + L^2/r^2), with tau in s, E dimensionless and L in cm^2 s^-1. Motion is allowed only where R(r) >= 0. The sign of dr/dtau reverses at an accessible simple turning root; multiple roots need separate treatment. A root alone does not establish a sign reversal.  
  `R(r) = r^4E^2-(r^2-2Mr)(L_z^2+r^2),\qquad \left(\frac{dr}{d\tau}\right)^2 = \frac{R(r)}{r^4} = E^2-\left(1-\frac{2M}{r}\right)\left(1+\frac{L_z^2}{r^2}\right)`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eq. 6 (with eq. 10) at a = 0, delta_1 = 1, Q = 0, p. 2; anchor: “&\Delta&[\mathcal{Q}+(L_z-aE)^2+\delta_1 r^2]\\”
- **gr.timelike-speed-at-infinity** [equation] — Asymptotic speed of a hyperbolic orbit, v^infinity = sqrt(1 - 1/E^2). For a hyperbolic timelike Schwarzschild geodesic (E > 1), the speed relative to static observers far from the star tends to v^infinity = sqrt(1 - 1/E^2) (c = 1); in CGS v^infinity = c sqrt(1 - E^(-2)). Equivalently, far from the star E = dt/dtau is the Lorentz factor (1 - v^2/c^2)^(-1/2). The asymptotic motion is radial: the transverse part r dphi/dt = (1 - 2M/r) L/(E r) -> 0 (from dphi/dtau = L/r^2 and dt/dtau = E/(1 - 2M/r)).  
  `v^\infty = \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{E^2}}\quad (c=1),\qquad E = \lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{dt}{d\tau} = \left[1-(v^{\infty})^2\right]^{-1/2}`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eqs. 1-3 and 8 at a = 0, r -> infinity, p. 2; anchor: “The equations of motion for the cyclic coordinates are”
- **gr.timelike-unbound-condition** [result] — Unbound (hyperbolic) timelike orbit: E > 1. Restrict to future-directed exterior geodesics, E > 0 (dt/dtau = E/(1 - 2M/r) > 0 for r > 2M). From (dr/dtau)^2 = E^2 - (1 - 2M/r)(1 + L^2/r^2), the right side tends to E^2 - 1 as r -> infinity. Such a geodesic reaches arbitrarily large r only if E >= 1. E > 1 (hyperbolic) gives a non-zero asymptotic radial rate, (dr/dtau)^2 -> E^2 - 1 > 0. E = 1 is the marginal (parabolic) case, with dr/dtau -> 0. For 0 < E < 1 the right side is negative at large r, so r is bounded. Without E > 0 the label E < 1 would include E < -1, for which (dr/dtau)^2 -> E^2 - 1 > 0 and the bound claim is false. E > 1 is necessary for the PRD camera's hyperbolic geodesic. It is not sufficient: the orbit must also turn at a periastron r_p > 2M rather than be captured (gr.timelike-periastron-cubic). The condition is the same in CGS (E dimensionless).  
  `\lim_{r\to\infty}\left(\frac{dr}{d\tau}\right)^2 = E^2-1;\qquad E>1\ \text{(hyperbolic)},\quad E=1\ \text{(parabolic)},\quad 0<E<1\ \text{(bound in } r\text{)}\qquad (E>0,\ \text{future-directed, } r>2M)`  
  src: `dexter_agol_2009_kerr` Sect. 2, eq. 6 at a = 0, delta_1 = 1, r -> infinity, p. 2; anchor: “&\Delta&[\mathcal{Q}+(L_z-aE)^2+\delta_1 r^2]\\”
- **gr.visible-fraction-cosine** [approximation] — Visible surface from the cosine relation. Setting alpha = 90 deg in the cosine relation gives the critical mu_v = -r_g/(R - r_g) and the visible fraction of the stellar surface S_v/(4 pi R^2) = (1 - mu_v)/2 = [2(1 - r_g/R)]^(-1); 0.75 for R = 3 r_g. Flat space gives 1/2.  
  `\mu_v=-\frac{r_g}{R-r_g},\qquad \frac{S_v}{4\pi R^2}=\frac{1-\mu_v}{2}=\left[2\left(1-\frac{r_g}{R}\right)\right]^{-1}`  
  src: `beloborodov_2002_ray_tracing` Sect. 3; anchor: “the surface is Sv /4πR2 = (1 − µv )/2 = [2(1 − rg /R)]−1”

## obs

- **obs.agis-astrometric-parameter-set** [equation] — AGIS: the six astrometric parameters at the reference epoch. The six astrometric parameters s_i are: alpha_i, the barycentric right ascension at the adopted reference epoch t_ep; delta_i, the barycentric declination at t_ep; varpi_i, the annual parallax at t_ep; mu_alpha*i = (d alpha_i/dt) cos delta_i, the proper motion in right ascension at t_ep; mu_delta,i = d delta_i/dt, the proper motion in declination at t_ep; and mu_ri = v_ri varpi_i / A_u, the 'radial proper motion' at t_ep, i.e. the radial velocity expressed in the same unit as the transverse proper motion (A_u = astronomical unit). The astrometric parameters refer to the ICRS and the time coordinate is TCB.  
  `\mu_{ri}=v_{ri}\varpi_i/A_\text{u}`  
  src: `lindegren_2012_agis` Sect. 3.2, parameter list (tex l.437); anchor: “the `radial proper motion' at epoch”
- **obs.agis-normal-triad** [equation] — Normal triad [p q r] of a source in the ICRS. In the normal triad r_i is the barycentric coordinate direction to the source at t_ep, p_i = <Z x r_i>, q_i = r_i x p_i (Z the ICRS pole). The ICRS components of these unit vectors are the columns of the matrix C'[p_i q_i r_i] = [[-sin alpha, -sin delta cos alpha, cos delta cos alpha],[cos alpha, -sin delta sin alpha, cos delta sin alpha],[0, cos delta, sin delta]]. The cross-product definition applies for abs(delta) < pi/2; at a pole choose alpha and construct the triad from the matrix.  
  `\tens{C}'[\vec{p}_i~\vec{q}_i~\vec{r}_i] = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin\alpha_i & -\sin\delta_i\cos\alpha_i & \cos\delta_i\cos\alpha_i \\ \cos\alpha_i & -\sin\delta_i\sin\alpha_i & \cos\delta_i\sin\alpha_i \\ 0 & \cos\delta_i & \sin\delta_i \end{bmatrix}`  
  src: `lindegren_2012_agis` Sect. 3.2, eq. (normal-triad) (tex l.470); anchor: “$\vec{p}_i=\langle\vec{Z}\times\vec{r}_i\rangle$, and”
- **obs.agis-standard-model-direction** [equation] — AGIS standard model: coordinate direction at time t (direction-vector form with perspective acceleration). - **obs.agis-standard-model-neglects-lighttime** [approximation] — AGIS standard model: what is neglected. The standard model can be derived by considering the uniform motion of the source in a purely classical framework, using Euclidean coordinates and neglecting the light propagation time from the source to the observer (except for the Roemer delay). The practical need to neglect most of the light-propagation time t - t_* (typically many years, and with a rate of change depending on the radial velocity, in general not known with sufficient accuracy) makes the transformation between kinematic and astrometric parameters non-trivial; the astrometric proper motions and radial velocity correspond to the 'apparent' quantities of Klioner (2003). To the accuracy of Gaia the model is stated to be accurate enough to model the observations to sub-microarcsec accuracy; when the astrometric parameters are to be interpreted in terms of the barycentric space velocity, some relativistic and light-propagation effects may come into play.

The six astrometric parameters are merely a transformation of the kinematic parameters into an equivalent set better suited for the analysis of observations.

These formulae should not be used for the actual propagation, but only to estimate the significance of the effects. With f_T = 1 + epsilon_T and f_V = 1 + epsilon_V, epsilon_T = -(mu_0^2 tau_A/(2 varpi_0)) t and epsilon_V = -(mu_0^2 tau_A/varpi_0) t. The relation that follows from (D.9) is Delta varpi = (1/2) varpi t Delta mu_r; this is algebra derived here from (D.9), not the printed identity. The position and parallax effects are quadratic in t, the proper-motion effects linear in t; all scale roughly as the third power of the space velocity. The strong cubic dependence on mu means light-time effects are mainly important for high-proper-motion stars. Example printed: Barnard's star (mu = 10357.70 mas/yr, varpi = 549.01 mas): at sigma_theta = 1 mas, negligible for t << 114 yr; at 1 microarcsec only for t << 3.6 yr.

The barycentric coordinate direction u = b/|b| and its time derivative, the proper motion vector mu = du/dt, are observable; they satisfy u'u = 1 and u'mu = 0 (four degrees of freedom). With the normal triad [p q r] at r (r = (cos delta cos alpha, cos delta sin alpha, sin delta), p = (-sin alpha, cos alpha, 0), q = (-sin delta cos alpha, -sin delta sin alpha, cos delta)) the proper motion components are the coordinates of mu along p and q: mu_alpha* = p'mu, mu_delta = q'mu, and mu = p mu_alpha* + q mu_delta. The motion may be regarded as uniform if |Delta theta| << sigma_theta. The dominant acceleration common to all stars is the Galactic one (differential acceleration relative to the SSB); at the Sun a_0 = V_0^2/R_0 ~ 2.5e-10 m s^-2 (R_0 ~ 8.4 kpc, V_0 ~ 254 km/s, as printed). - **obs.gaia-synthetic-mean-fluxes** [equation] — Synthetic mean energy fluxes per wavelength and per frequency through a passband. The mean energy flux per wavelength unit through a passband S is <f_lambda> = integral f_lambda S lambda d lambda / integral S lambda d lambda (VEGAMAG), and the mean energy flux per frequency unit is <f_nu> = integral f_lambda S lambda d lambda / integral S (c/lambda) d lambda (AB).  
  `<f_\lambda>\, = \frac{\int\, f_\lambda(\lambda) \,S(\lambda)\,\lambda \, {\rm d}\lambda }{\int\, S(\lambda)\,\lambda \, {\rm d}\lambda } \;\;(\mathrm{VEGAMAG}), \qquad <f_\nu>\, = \frac{\int\, f_\lambda(\lambda) \,S(\lambda)\,\lambda \, {\rm d}\lambda }{\int\, S(\lambda)\,\left(c/\lambda\right) \, {\rm d}\lambda }\;\;(\mathrm{AB})`  
  src: `riello_2021_gaia_photometry` Sect. 7, Eqs. (13)-(14), p. 17 (refs/riello_2021_gaia_photometry.txt:1108-1121); anchor: “for VEGAMAG, and the mean energy flux per frequency unit”

  `f_{550} = 3.62286\,10^{-11}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,nm^{-1}}\ \text{at}\ \lambda = 550.0\ \mathrm{nm}`  
  src: `riello_2021_gaia_photometry` Sect. 7, p. 17, text after Eq. (15) (refs/riello_2021_gaia_photometry.txt:1130-1136); anchor: “3.62286 10−11 W m−2 nm−1 at the wavelength λ = 550.0 nm,”
- **obs.gaia-vegamag-definition** [equation] — Gaia VEGAMAG synthetic magnitude. In the VEGAMAG system the synthetic magnitude in a Gaia band is m_VEG = -2.5 log <f_lambda> + 2.5 log [ integral f_lambda^Vg S lambda d lambda / integral S lambda d lambda ], where f_lambda^Vg is the Vega spectrum from the CALSPEC database (file alpha_lyr_mod_002.fits) rescaled so that f_550 = 3.62286e-11 W m^-2 nm^-1 at 550.0 nm, the flux assumed for an unreddened A0V star with V = 0.  
  `m_{VEG} = -2.5 \log <f_\lambda> + 2.5 \log \frac{\int f_\lambda^{Vg}(\lambda) S(\lambda)\lambda \, {\rm d}\lambda } {\int S(\lambda)\lambda \, {\rm d}\lambda }`  
  src: `riello_2021_gaia_photometry` Sect. 7, Eq. (15), p. 17 (refs/riello_2021_gaia_photometry.txt:1125-1143); anchor: “where fλVg (λ) is the Vega spectrum from the CALSPEC Cal-”
- **obs.gaia-xp-absolute-calibration** [datum] — SPSS flux scale and grey-normalised internally calibrated mean-spectrum residuals. SPSS/PVL/NGSL validation residuals: P16–P84 mostly within ±2% above approximately 400 nm; grey-rescaled median residual curves at the ±1% level, with magnitude-dependent deviations. The 111 SPSS used for the absolute calibration are calibrated to the CALSPEC scale with flux accuracy of about 1% (refs/montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp.txt:197-202). This passage does not establish +-1% absolute accuracy of the externally calibrated spectra.  
  src: `montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp` refs/montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp.txt:197-202 (SPSS, Sect. 3 Calibrators); refs/montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp.txt:1042-1071 (residuals); anchor: “sources, calibrated to the CALSPEC”
- **obs.gaia-xp-ecs-definition** [definition] — Externally calibrated BP/RP spectrum (ECS). Once the instrument model is fitted, it can be used in the opposite direction to transform an internally calibrated mean BP/RP spectrum into a wavelength- and flux-calibrated spectrum, called an externally calibrated spectrum (ECS). The instrument model solves simultaneously for the flux and wavelength calibrations and the line spread function, and its application reduces the photon mixing inherent to the slitless spectra, enhancing the effective spectral resolution of ECS.  
  `\text{ECS: wavelength- and flux-calibrated mean BP/RP spectrum}`  
  src: `montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp` Sect. 1 Introduction (refs/montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp.txt:126-140); anchor: “we call an externally calibrated spectrum (ECS).”
- **obs.gaia-xp-ecs-spd-sed-units** [equation] — ECS: spectral photon distribution and SED units, and usable wavelength range. The reconstructed externally calibrated spectrum is given as the spectral photon distribution n_p in photons s^-1 m^-2 nm^-1 (Eq. 33) and as the SED f_lambda in W m^-2 nm^-1 (Eq. 34), reconstructed by two distinct matrix equations, n_p = (D_phi^P H V_C^T) b and f_lambda = (D_phi^E H V_C^T) b. The sampling wavelength grid must be limited to [330, 650] nm for BP and [635, 1050] nm for RP to avoid large errors in the reconstructed spectra. The two partial spectra are combined into a single distribution by a weighted mean in the overlap region [lambda_lo, lambda_hi] with linear weights w_BP = 1 - (lambda - lambda_lo)/(lambda_hi - lambda_lo), w_RP = 1 - w_BP. The numerical conversion factor inside the design matrix D^E is unresolved and is not certified here.  
  `\mathbf n_p=(D_\varphi^P H V_C^T)\mathbf b\ [\mathrm{photons\,s^{-1}\,m^{-2}\,nm^{-1}}],\qquad \mathbf f_\lambda=(D_\varphi^E H V_C^T)\mathbf b\ [\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,nm^{-1}}]`  
  src: `montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp` Sect. 5, Eqs. (33)–(36), p. 8 (refs/montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp.txt:526-550); anchor: “which is the SED in units of $\rm W m^{-2} nm^{-1}$.”
- **obs.gaia-xp-sampled-subset** [datum] — Gaia DR3 XP mean spectra: counts and the sampled ECS subset (G < 15). XP mean spectra are published for 219,197,643 sources, mostly sources with G brighter than 17.65 mag and more than 15 CCD transits for both XP. All are given in a continuous (basis-function) representation. For a selected subset of sources with BP and RP spectral data that includes only sources brighter than G = 15 mag (the exact list is obtained by selecting gaia_source.has_xp_sampled = 't'; this is not stated to be every G < 15 source) the XP spectra are also provided in a sampled representation on a default grid as externally calibrated spectra in absolute flux and wavelength systems; for other sources ECS can be computed with GaiaXPy on a user-defined wavelength grid.  
  src: `montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp` Appendix B (refs/montegriffo_2023_gaia_xp.txt:1932-1959); anchor: “BP and RP mean spectra are published for 219,197,643 sources.”

The new Hipparcos reduction reports a basic five-parameter astrometric solution that was sufficient for 102 072 out of 117 955 stars. The validation paper's Table 1 tabulates parallax (varpi) and the proper-motion components mu_alpha* and mu_delta with formal errors for HIP 70 and HIP 71 (old versus new reduction, units mas and mas/yr). - **obs.hipparcos-observed-magnitude-range** [datum] — Hipparcos observed magnitude range: stars from magnitude -1 to 12.5 were observed. The paper's abstract states the new catalogue is claimed to have accuracies better, by up to a factor 4, for nearly all stars brighter than Hp = 8. - **obs.hipparcos-optical-realization-icrs** [datum] — Hipparcos 1997 catalogue as the optical realization of the ICRS. The Hipparcos catalogue as published in 1997 serves as the optical realization of the International Celestial Reference System (ICRS). The validation paper compares the new reduction with it in positions and proper motions and finds relative rotations and spins smaller than the accuracy with which the published catalogue was linked to the ICRS (spin components in mas/yr: omega_x = -0.001 +/- 0.003, omega_y = -0.005 +/- 0.003, omega_z = +0.006 +/- 0.003).

- **obs.mellinger-background-and-star-content** [datum] — Mellinger 2009: which light is removed and which kept; stars are NOT removed. Light pollution, airglow, zodiacal light and tropospheric scattering (I_bad) were removed using Pioneer 10/11 space-probe sky-background data (Gordon et al. 1998) for the retained component I_good = I_ISL + I_DGL + I_EBL (integrated starlight of unresolved stars, diffuse galactic light, extragalactic background). The model is I = S + I_bad + I_good with S the flux of point sources or resolved diffuse objects; I_bad is estimated by a strong median filter of (I - I_good) and subtracted, leaving S + I_good. Stars were not removed: the panorama shows stars to approx. 14 mag, plus the Magellanic Clouds, M31 and solar-system objects ('No attempt was made to remove or avoid solar system objects invisible to the naked eye'). The Pioneer data do not cover the whole sky (excluded within 70 deg of the Sun for Pioneer 10 and 45 deg for Pioneer 11); missing data were filled from Leinert et al. (1998) points on a 10 x 10 degree grid and a bicubic spline interpolation.

- **obs.mellinger-resolution-and-range** [datum] — Mellinger 2009 panorama: pixel scale, limiting magnitude, dynamic range. An optical (RGB) all-sky mosaic image with an image scale of 36 arcsec/pixel (36000 x 18000 pixels, 360 x 180 degrees, 648 Megapixel), a limiting magnitude of approx. 14 mag and an 18 bit dynamic range, assembled from 70 fields (each covering 40 x 27 degrees) imaged over 21 months from dark-sky locations in South Africa, Texas and Michigan; more than 3000 individual CCD images. Stars brighter than +0.7 mag are saturated; the faintest visible stars are approx. 14 mag. Floating-point maps are 32-bit, about 2.5 GByte per colour channel; an OpenEXR half-precision version is 'in preparation'.
