## opacity

- **opacity.approx-ff-non-born-correction** [approximation] — Born free-free Coulomb logarithm rescaled to the non-Born Gaunt factor. Because the Born approximation is accurate only for photon energies far above binding energies, PC03 multiplies Lambda^ff_alpha by the ratio of the non-Born Gaunt factor g-bar_ff (Hummer 1988) to g-bar_Born = (sqrt 3/pi) Lambda^ff_cl, so that the B = 0 limit recovers the non-Born Gaunt factor.  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` p. 966, paragraph before Sect. 5; anchor: “As well known, the Born approximation is accurate”
- **opacity.approx-mode-beta-small-polarizability** [approximation] — Small-polarisability form of beta. When plasma and vacuum polarisabilities are small, beta reduces to a form in the Hermitian cyclic polarisabilities chi^H_alpha and the vacuum combination (q + m)/(2 pi).  
  `\beta \approx \frac{2\chi^{\rm H}_0-\chi^{\rm H}_{+1}-\chi^{\rm H}_{-1}+(q+m)/(2\pi)}{2\left(\chi^{\rm H}_{+1}-\chi^{\rm H}_{-1}\right)}\,\frac{\sin^2\theta_B}{\cos\theta_B}`  
  src: `potekhin_lai_chabrier_ho_2004_polarization` eq. 22 (p. 6); anchor: “case where the plasma and vacuum polarizabilities are”
- **opacity.approx-vacuum-low-energy** [approximation] — Vacuum polarisation from the Euler-Heisenberg Lagrangian, added linearly. The vacuum polarisation coefficients are computed from the Euler-Heisenberg effective Lagrangian in the low-energy limit and, when small, the vacuum polarisability is added linearly to the plasma polarisability; mode conversion across the vacuum resonance is a separate transfer problem.  
  src: `potekhin_lai_chabrier_ho_2004_polarization` Appendix (p. 9), and Sect. 2.1 (p. 2); anchor: “the Euler-Heisenberg effective Lagrangian can be applied.”
- **opacity.coulomb-log-born-magnetic** [equation] — Magnetic Coulomb logarithm in the Born approximation. Coulomb logarithm Lambda^ff_alpha for free-free absorption in a quantising field, Born approximation, electron scattering off a fixed Coulomb centre (infinite proton mass); a function only of u and beta_e, summed over cyclotron harmonics n.  
  `\Lambda^{\rm ff}_\alpha = \frac34 e^{u/2}\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\int_0^\infty Q^\alpha_n(\beta_e,u,y)\,dy,\quad Q^\alpha_n = \frac{y}{\zeta}\frac{A^\alpha_n}{\left[(y+\theta+\zeta)\sinh(\beta_e/2)\right]^{|n|}},\quad A^0_n = \frac{x_nK_1(x_n)}{y+\beta_e/4},\quad A^{\pm1}_n = \frac{y+\theta+|n|\zeta}{\zeta^2}K_0(x_n),\quad \zeta=\sqrt{1+2\theta y+y^2},\quad \theta=\frac{1+\exp(-\beta_e)}{1-\exp(-\beta_e)},\quad x_n=|u-n\beta_e|\sqrt{0.25+y/\beta_e}`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eqs. 44a-e (p. 963); anchor: “Equation (44) has been derived assuming that an elec-”
- **opacity.coulomb-log-classical** [equation] — Classical (Born, B = 0) Coulomb logarithm. Maxwell average of the Born free-free cross section gives the classical Coulomb logarithm Lambda_cl = e^(u/2) K_0(u/2), with K_0 the modified Bessel function; Lambda = (pi/sqrt 3) g-bar relates it to the Gaunt factor.  
  `\Lambda^{\rm ff}_{\rm cl} = e^{u/2}K_0(u/2),\qquad \Lambda = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt3}\,\bar g`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eq. 43 (p. 963); Lambda = (pi/sqrt 3) g-bar in text before eq. 41; anchor: “classical Coulomb logarithm”
- **opacity.cyclotron-energy-electron** [equation] — Electron cyclotron energy. The electron cyclotron energy (nonrelativistic Landau-level spacing; relativistic levels: Lai 2001 Eq. 2.12) as a function of field strength: hbar omega_ce = hbar e B / (m_e c) = 11.577 B_12 keV.  
  `\hbar\omega_{\rm ce} = \hbar\frac{eB}{m_e c} = 11.577\,B_{12}\ {\rm keV}`  
  src: `lai_2001_strong_B_review` Eq. 1.1 (PDF p. 2); anchor: “cyclotron energy (the Landau level spacing) of the electron is”
- **opacity.damping-frequencies** [equation] — Damping frequencies of the cyclotron resonances. Electron damping nu_{e,alpha} is the sum of the free-free absorption frequency and the natural radiative width nu^s_e; the proton damping nu_{p,alpha} is the sum of the ion free-free term (m_e/m_p) nu^ff_alpha, the natural width nu^s_p and the proton-proton term nu^pp_alpha.  
  `\nu_{e,\alpha} = \nu^{\rm ff}_\alpha + \nu^{\rm s}_{e},\quad \nu^{\rm s}_{e} = \frac23\frac{e^2}{m_e c^3}\omega^2,\quad \nu_{p,\alpha} = \nu^{\rm ff,p}_\alpha + \nu^{\rm s}_{p} + \nu^{\rm pp}_\alpha,\quad \nu^{\rm ff,p}_\alpha \equiv \frac{m_e}{m_p}\nu^{\rm ff}_\alpha,\quad \nu^{\rm s}_{p} = \frac{2e^2\omega^2}{3m_pc^3}`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eqs. 38, 39 (p. 963), eq. 53 and text after eq. 52 (p. 964-965); anchor: “determined by the sum of the effective frequencies for”
- **opacity.ff-cross-section-cold-plasma** [equation] — Free-free cross section in the cold-plasma, infinite-proton-mass form. Classical cold-plasma free-free absorption by electrons: a Lorentzian cyclotron factor times 4 pi e^2/(m_e c) times the effective collision frequency nu^ff_alpha.  
  `\sigma^{\rm ff}_\alpha = \frac{1}{(\omega+\alpha\omega_{\rm ce})^2+\nu_{e,\alpha}^2}\,\frac{4\pi e^2}{m_e c}\,\nu^{\rm ff}_\alpha(\omega)`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eq. 37 (p. 963); anchor: “In the classical cold plasma approximation (e.g.,”
- **opacity.ff-cross-section-finite-proton-mass** [equation] — Free-free cross section with finite proton mass (PC03 main result). Free-free photoabsorption cross section with both electron and proton cyclotron resonances and the proton motion; for alpha = +/-1 it is suppressed by about (omega/omega_cp)^2 at omega << omega_cp and is reproduced for accurate Appendix-B results when Lambda^ff_alpha in nu^ff_alpha is multiplied by an order-unity quantum correction factor.  
  `\sigma^{\rm ff}_\alpha \approx \frac{\omega^2}{(\omega+\alpha\omega_{\rm ce})^2(\omega-\alpha\omega_{\rm cp})^2+\omega^2\tilde\nu_\alpha^2}\,\frac{4\pi e^2\nu^{\rm ff}_\alpha}{m_ec},\qquad \tilde\nu_\alpha = \nu^{\rm ff}_\alpha+\left(1+\frac{\alpha\omega_{\rm ce}}{\omega}\right)\nu_p+\left(1-\frac{\alpha\omega_{\rm cp}}{\omega}\right)\nu_e`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eqs. 51, 52 (p. 964); anchor: “glecting the tiny shift of the position of the cyclotron”
- **opacity.field-atomic-b0** [constant] — Atomic magnetic field B_0. The atomic unit of magnetic field strength B_0 = m_e^2 c e^3 / hbar^3; fields B > B_0 are called strong (hbar omega_ce exceeds one atomic unit of energy).  
  `B_0 = \frac{m_e^2 c\, e^3}{\hbar^3}`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` p. 955 (Sect. 1); anchor: “the field strength B is higher than B0 = m2e c e3 /~3 =”
- **opacity.field-qed-bq** [constant] — QED critical field B_Q. The relativistic (QED) critical field B_Q = m_e^2 c^3 / (e hbar) = 4.414e13 G, at which hbar omega_ce = m_e c^2; the dimensionless parameter b = B / B_Q governs vacuum polarisation.  
  `B_Q = \frac{m_e^2 c^3}{e\hbar}`  
  src: `potekhin_lai_chabrier_ho_2004_polarization` Appendix, text before eq. A1 (p. 9); anchor: “BQ = m2e c3 /e~ = 4.414 × 1013 G”
- **opacity.mode-absorption-opacity** [equation] — Absorption opacity in a normal mode. The absorption opacity of normal mode j at propagation angle theta_B is the sum over basic polarisations of the squared cyclic components of the mode vector times the basic cross section per hydrogen mass; for hydrogen the cross section combines bound and free-free parts through x_H.  
  `\kappa^{\rm a}_j(\theta_B) = m_H^{-1}\sum_{\alpha=-1}^{1}|e_{j,\alpha}(\theta_B)|^2\,\sigma^{\rm a}_\alpha,\qquad \sigma^{\rm a}_\alpha = x_H(\sigma^{\rm bb}_\alpha+\sigma^{\rm bf}_\alpha)+(1-x_H)(\sigma^{\rm ff}_\alpha+\sigma^{\rm pp}_\alpha)`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eqs. 27, 31 (p. 959); anchor: “At a fixed photon frequency ω, the absorption opacity”
- **opacity.mode-parameter-beta** [equation] — Polarisation parameter beta (exact form). The polarisation parameter beta entering K_j, written through the dielectric elements, vacuum coefficients and the propagation angle.  
  `\beta = \frac{\eta'-\varepsilon'+g^2/\varepsilon'+\eta' m/(1+\hat a)}{2g}\;\frac{\varepsilon'}{\eta'}\;\frac{\sin^2\theta_B}{\cos\theta_B}`  
  src: `potekhin_lai_chabrier_ho_2004_polarization` Eq. 21 (p. 5); definitions (p. 6); anchor: “θB is the angle between B and the z axis, and (see”
- **opacity.mode-parameters-k** [equation] — Mode parameters K_j and K_{z,j}. The mode parameters in terms of the dielectric elements, the vacuum magnetisation coefficient m and the polarisation parameter beta; epsilon' = epsilon + a_hat and eta' = eta + a_hat + q include vacuum.  
  `K_j = \beta\left\{1+(-1)^j\left[1+\frac{1}{\beta^2}+\frac{m}{1+\hat a}\frac{\sin^2\theta_B}{\beta^2}\right]^{1/2}\right\},\quad K_{z,j} = -\frac{(\varepsilon'-\eta')K_j\cos\theta_B+g}{\varepsilon'\sin^2\theta_B+\eta'\cos^2\theta_B}\,\sin\theta_B,\quad \varepsilon'=\varepsilon+\hat a,\ \eta'=\eta+\hat a+q`  
  src: `potekhin_lai_chabrier_ho_2004_polarization` eqs. 19, 20 and text after eq. 21 (pp. 5-6); anchor: “of the dielectric and magnetic tensors as”
- **opacity.mode-polarization-vector** [equation] — Normal-mode polarisation vector. Polarisation vectors of the extraordinary (j = 1) and ordinary (j = 2) normal modes in the frame with z along the photon wave vector and B in the x-z plane, parametrised by K_j and K_{z,j}.  
  `(e^j_x,e^j_y,e^j_z) = \left(1+K_j^2+K_{z,j}^2\right)^{-1/2}\left(iK_j,\ 1,\ iK_{z,j}\right)`  
  src: `potekhin_lai_chabrier_ho_2004_polarization` eq. 18 (p. 5); anchor: “where j = 1, 2 correspond to the extraordinary mode (X-”
- **opacity.mode-scattering-opacity** [equation] — Scattering opacity between normal modes. Opacity for scattering from mode j into mode j' at angle theta_B, built from the cyclic mode-vector components and the polarisation cross sections; the total scattering opacity of mode j is kappa^s_{j1} + kappa^s_{j2} and the extinction opacity is kappa^a_j + kappa^s_j.  
  `\kappa^{\rm s}_{jj'}(\theta_B) = \frac34\sum_{\alpha=-1}^{1}|e_{j,\alpha}(\theta_B)|^2\,\frac{\sigma^{\rm s}_\alpha}{m_H}\int_0^\pi|e_{j',\alpha}(\theta_B')|^2\sin\theta_B'\,d\theta_B',\quad \sigma^{\rm s}_\alpha=\sigma^{\rm s,e}_\alpha+\sigma^{\rm s,p}_\alpha,\quad \kappa_j=\kappa^{\rm a}_j+\kappa^{\rm s}_{j1}+\kappa^{\rm s}_{j2}`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eq. 28 and text after it (p. 959); anchor: “from mode j into mode j ′ can be presented as (e.g.,”
- **opacity.plasma-frequency** [equation] — Electron plasma frequency. The electron plasma energy hbar omega_pl in terms of n_e, with its numerical form for hydrogen (28.7 sqrt(rho_0) eV). Normal-mode propagation is described at photon energies hbar omega well above hbar omega_pl.  
  `\hbar\omega_{\rm pl} = \left(\frac{4\pi\hbar^2 e^2 n_e}{m_e}\right)^{1/2} \approx 28.7\,\rho_0^{1/2}\ {\rm eV}`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eq. 24 (p. 958); anchor: “where ωpl is the electron plasma frequency and ρ0 ≡”
- **opacity.quantisation-parameter-beta-e** [equation] — Electron quantisation parameter beta_e. The ratio of the electron cyclotron energy to k_B T. Values beta_e >> 1 mean the field is quantising; beta_e < 1 means the nonmagnetic Gaunt factor applies.  
  `\beta_e = \hbar\omega_{\rm ce}/k_B T \approx 134.3\,B_{12}/T_6`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` Eq. 1 (p. 955); Sect. 4.3.1 (p. 963); anchor: “~ωce /kB T ≈ 134.3 B12/T6 ,”
- **opacity.quantising-density-rho-b** [equation] — Density bound rho_B for strongly quantising fields. A field is strongly quantising (most electrons on the ground Landau level) when zeta_e >> 1 and the density is below rho_B = m_i / (pi^2 sqrt(2) a_m^3 Z) = 7045 (A/Z) B_12^(3/2) g cm^-3.  
  `\rho_B = \frac{m_i}{\pi^2\sqrt{2}\,a_m^3 Z} = 7045\,\frac{A}{Z}\,B_{12}^{3/2}\ {\rm g\,cm^{-3}}`  
  src: `potekhin_ho_chabrier_2016_review` eq. 2.13 (p. 6); anchor: “most electrons reside on the ground Landau level, and the field”
- **opacity.scattering-electron-magnetic** [equation] — Magnetic electron scattering cross section. Electron scattering cross section for basic polarisation alpha (0, +/-1) outside a narrow range around omega_ce; the alpha = -1 component has the electron cyclotron resonance, and sigma^s,e_alpha -> sigma_T when omega_ce << omega and nu_e,alpha << omega.  
  `\sigma^{\rm s,e}_\alpha = \frac{\omega^2}{(\omega+\alpha\omega_{\rm ce})^2+\nu_{e,\alpha}^2}\,\sigma_T`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eq. 33 (p. 961); anchor: “Outside of a narrow (about the Doppler”
- **opacity.scattering-proton-magnetic** [equation] — Magnetic proton scattering cross section. Proton scattering cross section for basic polarisation alpha; the alpha = +1 component has a resonance at omega_cp, and it is negligible without a field.  
  `\sigma^{\rm s,p}_\alpha = \left(\frac{m_e}{m_p}\right)^2\frac{\omega^2}{(\omega-\alpha\omega_{\rm cp})^2+\nu_{p,\alpha}^2}\,\sigma_T`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` eq. 34 (p. 961); anchor: “The scattering by the protons, which is completely neg-”
- **opacity.thomson-cross-section** [equation] — Nonmagnetic Thomson cross section. The nonmagnetic Thomson cross section sigma_T = (8 pi/3)(e^2/(m_e c^2))^2.  
  `\sigma_T = \frac{8\pi}{3}\left(\frac{e^2}{m_e c^2}\right)^2`  
  src: `potekhin_chabrier_2003_ff_opacity` text after eq. 33 (p. 961); anchor: “where σT = (8π/3)(e2 /me c2 )2 is the nonmagnetic Thom-”
- **opacity.thomson-opacity-mcphac** [equation] — Reduced Thomson scattering opacity (McPHAC). The Thomson scattering opacity per unit mass for ionisation fraction f_ion, which for fully ionised hydrogen (f_ion = 1) is sigma_T / (m_p + m_e).  
  `\sigma_{T,r} = \frac{f_{\rm ion}\,\sigma_T}{f_{\rm ion}(m_p+m_e)+(1-f_{\rm ion})\,m_H}`  
  src: `haakonsen_2012_mcphac` eq. 11 (p. 4); anchor: “For an ionization fraction fion at a given depth, the reduced”
- **opacity.vacuum-coeffs-heyl-hernquist** [equation] — Vacuum polarisation coefficients for arbitrary field (Heyl-Hernquist form). The Heyl and Hernquist (1997) result for a_hat, a_hat + q and m reduced to a function X(xi) of the Gamma function, with xi = 1/b.  
  `\hat a=\frac{\alpha_f}{2\pi}\left[\xi X(\xi)-2\int_1^\xi X(\xi')\,d\xi'-0.0329199\right],\quad \hat a+q=\frac{\alpha_f}{2\pi}\left[\frac{2}{9\xi^2}-\frac23X'(\xi)\right],\quad m=\frac{\alpha_f}{2\pi}\left[\xi X(\xi)-\xi^2X'(\xi)\right],\quad X(\xi)=2\ln\Gamma(\xi/2)-\frac{1}{3\xi}-\ln\frac{4\pi}{\xi}+\xi+\xi\ln\frac{2}{\xi},\quad X'(\xi)=\frac{dX}{d\xi},\ \xi=b^{-1}`  
  src: `potekhin_lai_chabrier_ho_2004_polarization` eqs. A2-A6 (p. 9); anchor: “can be reduced to the following more convenient form:”
- **opacity.vacuum-coeffs-weak-field** [equation] — Vacuum polarisation coefficients, weak-field limit. In the limit b << 1 the vacuum polarisation coefficients are a_hat = -2 alpha_f b^2/(45 pi), q = 7 alpha_f b^2/(45 pi), m = -4 alpha_f b^2/(45 pi) (Adler 1971), with b = B/B_Q.  
  `\hat a = -\frac{2\alpha_f}{45\pi}b^2,\qquad q=\frac{7\alpha_f}{45\pi}b^2,\qquad m=-\frac{4\alpha_f}{45\pi}b^2`  
  src: `potekhin_lai_chabrier_ho_2004_polarization` eq. A1 (p. 9); anchor: “the vacuum polarization coefficients are given by (Adler 1971)”
- **opacity.vacuum-resonance-density** [equation] — Vacuum resonance density. A photon of energy E traversing the atmosphere density gradient meets the vacuum resonance at density rho_V = 0.96 Y_e^-1 E_1^2 B_14^2 f_B^-2 g cm^-3 (inverse of the resonance energy relation).  
  `\rho_V = 0.96\,Y_e^{-1}E_1^{2}B_{14}^{2}f_B^{-2}\ {\rm g\,cm^{-3}}`  
  src: `van_adelsberg_lai_2006_magnetic_atm` Eq. 2 (p. 4); anchor: “traversing the density gradient of a NS atmosphere. The photon will encounter th”

## pipeline

- **pipeline.atmosphere-structure** [pipeline] — Atmosphere structure: hydrostatics and equation of state. Given T(y) and surface gravity g (cm s^-2), compute P = g y (dyn cm^-2) when radiative acceleration is neglected, otherwise integrate dP_g/dy = g - g_rad and the density rho(P, T) (g cm^-3) of fully ionised hydrogen from the ideal-gas EOS rho = m_p P / (2 k_B T), flagging where Landau quantisation (rho < rho_B) or non-ideality would matter; also provides the density scale height H_rho (cm), defined along the vertical (not along the ray) unless a caller converts with the ray angle.  
  src: `PRD` Milestones, 3; anchor: “audit and salvage the v1 atmosphere solver”
- **pipeline.camera-tetrad-projection** [pipeline] — Camera tetrad and pixel-to-photon-momentum projection. At each camera event of pipeline.camera-worldline build the camera's orthonormal tetrad e_(a)^cam: the static-observer tetrad of gr.static-tetrad, e_(t) = [c (1 - r_g/r)^(1/2)]^(-1) d/dt, e_(r) = (1 - r_g/r)^(1/2) d/dr, e_(theta) = r^(-1) d/dtheta, e_(phi) = (r sin theta)^(-1) d/dphi, boosted by the local Lorentz transformation (gr.tetrad-lorentz-transformation, the sign giving e_(0)^cam = gamma (e_(0) + beta_cam hat v_cam^a e_(a))) to the camera four-velocity u_cam = c gamma (e_(0) + beta_cam hat v_cam), whose speed beta_cam and direction hat v_cam relative to the static observer are read off the worldline's u^mu (gr.camera-four-velocity-static-frame); e_(0)^cam = u_cam/c. Pixel mapping (gr.camera-projection-convention): optical axis a_cam, image-right u_x and image-up u_y with u_x x u_y = -a_cam; a pixel offset (dx, dy) from the optical-axis pixel gives r_pix = (dx^2 + dy^2)^(1/2), phi_field = atan2(dy, dx) and the field angle theta_field = arctan(r_pix/f_cam) (pinhole, theta_field < pi/2) or theta_field = r_pix/f_cam (equidistant), with f_cam > 0 in pixels; at r_pix = 0, set N_cam = a_cam without evaluating atan2; equidistant pixels require 0 ≤ theta_field ≤ pi; the pixel's sky direction is N_cam = cos theta_field a_cam + sin theta_field (cos phi_field u_x + sin phi_field u_y). Direction convention: N_cam points toward the apparent source of the incoming ray (N of James et al. 2015 eq. A.8); the photon propagates along -N_cam, with four-momentum p = (h nu_cam/c)(e_(0)^cam - N^a e_(a)^cam), so h nu_cam = -p_mu u^mu_cam, and coordinate components p^mu = p^(i) e_(i)^mu (gr.tetrad-vector-components). Aberration between the camera and static frames is this one boost (gr.camera-aberration, n_F the static-frame propagation direction). From p_mu return, per pixel and frequency, the ray's conserved constants (gr.null-geodesic-constants: p_t, p_phi in its own orbit plane, impact parameter b = |p_phi/p_t| c in cm), its orbit plane (the plane through r = 0 containing the camera position and the spatial direction of p; for a radial ray (b = 0), choose a fixed auxiliary orbit plane) and its initial radial branch; the static-frame sky angle of gr.observer-sky-angle is a consistency check. Pointing for a still: image-up u_y is -e_(theta)^cam (the orbit normal along +L_z of pipeline.camera-worldline, unchanged by boosts in the orbit plane), orthogonalised against a_cam; in tracking mode a_cam is the camera-frame image, through gr.camera-aberration, of the static-frame inward radial direction -e_(r) (the star's centre). This M1 computation supports tracking only; fixed-inertial requests raise until a transport-law dependency exists. Each frame supplies the projection and positive f_cam. gr.disk-angular-radius is a distant-static verification target only.  
  src: `PRD` The shot, Frame; anchor: “the camera's local tetrad. Aberration, Doppler, and gravitational”
- **pipeline.camera-worldline** [pipeline] — Camera worldline (hyperbolic timelike geodesic). Integrate the camera worldline as an unbound (hyperbolic) timelike geodesic of the Schwarzschild exterior of pipeline.ns-exterior-spacetime, parameterised by camera proper time tau_prop (s). Mass: the star's gravitational mass is a labelled parameter m_star_N := GM/(GM)^N_sun (the nominal-solar-mass ratio defined through GM; the symbol m is reserved for column density); r_g = 2GM/c^2 is computed from the product GM = m_star_N (GM)^N_sun with (GM)^N_sun = 1.3271244e26 cm^3 s^-2 (const.gm-sun-nominal-cgs), and M in grams, where needed, is M ≈ m_star_N × 1.98841e33 g with CODATA 2018 G (const.m-sun-nominal-cgs, not an IAU nominal quantity). Inputs: the conserved specific energy E-tilde = (1 - r_g/r) dt/dtau_prop > 1 (dimensionless; the unbound condition of gr.timelike-unbound-condition), or equivalently the speed at infinity v_inf = c (1 - E-tilde^-2)^(1/2) (gr.timelike-speed-at-infinity), and the periastron radius r_peri (cm; PRD default about 100 km). The specific angular momentum L-tilde = r^2 dphi_Sch/dtau_prop (cm^2 s^-1) follows from L-tilde^2 = c^2 r_peri^2 [E-tilde^2/(1 - r_g/r_peri) - 1] (gr.timelike-angular-momentum-from-periastron); the run raises unless r_peri > max(R, r_g) and r_peri is the largest real root of the periastron cubic and a simple root with d\mathcal{R}/dr(r_peri) > 0 (gr.timelike-periastron-cubic), so that the orbit turns at r_peri, is not captured, and does not intersect the star. Orientation convention: the orbit lies in the Schwarzschild equatorial plane theta_Sch = pi/2 (Carter constant Q = 0), L_z = +|L-tilde| so phi_Sch increases along the orbit, phi_Sch = 0 and tau_prop = 0 at periastron, and tau_prop increases to the future (E-tilde > 0). Equations: (dr/dtau_prop)^2 = c^2 E-tilde^2 - (1 - r_g/r)(c^2 + L-tilde^2/r^2) (gr.timelike-radial-equation-schwarzschild), dt/dtau_prop = E-tilde (1 - r_g/r)^(-1), dphi_Sch/dtau_prop = L-tilde/r^2; the inbound branch dr/dtau_prop < 0 holds for tau_prop < 0 and the outbound branch for tau_prop > 0. Proper time is the unsigned two-leg quadrature dtau_prop = |dr|/(c^2 E-tilde^2 - (1 - r_g/r)(c^2 + L-tilde^2/r^2))^(1/2), integrated with increasing r on each leg, r_peri -> r_start inbound and r_peri -> r_end outbound, with the integrable 1/(r - r_peri)^(1/2) endpoint singularity regularised (gr.timelike-proper-time-quadrature). Finite r_start, r_end > r_peri are supplied inputs; the caller verifies the unresolved-endpoint criterion using the moving-camera image and stated PSF. Output: x^mu(tau_prop) = (t, r, theta_Sch, phi_Sch) and u^mu(tau_prop) = dx^mu/dtau_prop, with g_mu nu u^mu u^nu = -c^2 checked at every output event (fail loud).  
  src: `PRD` The shot, Camera; anchor: “on a hyperbolic timelike geodesic of the Schwarzschild spacetime of”
- **pipeline.display-colour** [pipeline] — Spectral radiance to CIE XYZ to linear and encoded sRGB. Integrate the pixel spectral radiance I_lambda (erg s^-1 cm^-2 nm^-1 sr^-1, I_lambda = I_nu |dnu/dlambda| = I_nu c/lambda^2 with the nm conversion, lambda = c/nu) against the CIE 1931 2-degree colour matching functions over 360-830 nm to get X, Y, Z (absolute, then scaled by exposure); convert XYZ to linear sRGB with the matrix obtained by inverting the primaries/D65 matrix built from the sRGB chromaticities; clip to gamut; apply the sRGB transfer function and quantise to 8-bit code values. Clipping and quantisation are lossy; the original HDR data is retained, and the inverse path (code value to linear sRGB) is only an approximate decode.  
  src: `PRD` The shot, Primary output; anchor: “Display images and video are derived with a stated camera,”
- **pipeline.earth-photometry** [pipeline] — Earth-distance photometry harness (R5). Render the star from a static camera at d = 123 pc with the same geodesic, frequency-shift and surface-radiance computations, integrate the point-source flux F_nu (erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1), apply interstellar extinction (N_H from either obs.rxj1856-ho2007-nh or obs.rxj1856-xray-nh-chandra, alternatives and never simultaneous), fold through the HST filter throughputs, and convert to STMAG (STMAG requires F_lambda with explicit per-Angstrom units); compare with the published optical/UV magnitudes and flux densities of RX J1856 within their errors, for each surface model. Also provides the forward model for the parameter fit.  
  src: `PRD` Requirements, R5; anchor: “A render from 123 pc reproduces the HST optical/UV magnitudes of RX J1856”
- **pipeline.free-free-opacity** [pipeline] — Free-free absorption (B = 0 and magnetic). Free-free absorption cross sections sigma^ff_alpha(omega) (cm^2) per cyclic polarisation component alpha = -1, 0, +1 for fully ionised hydrogen: at B = 0 the undamped Kramers form (negligible damping required) times the thermally averaged Gaunt factor with stimulated emission; at B > 0 the PC03 Eq. 51 approximation with finite proton mass with effective collision frequencies built from the magnetic Coulomb logarithms Lambda_alpha^ff (Born, rescaled by the non-Born Gaunt ratio) and the damping frequencies.  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “surface emission as spectral, angular, and polarised radiance from (a)”
- **pipeline.frequency-shift** [pipeline] — Gravitational, Doppler and aberration shift of I_nu. For each ray, compute the frequency ratio g = nu_cam/nu_em = (p . u_cam)/(p . u_em) from the photon four-momentum and the emitter (static surface or distant sky) and camera four-velocities, and transform the specific intensity by I_nu,cam(nu_cam) = g^3 I_nu,em(nu_cam/g), i.e. for the static case I_nu,obs(nu) = (1+z)^(-3) I_nu,em((1+z)nu) (I_nu/nu^3 invariant). For a static camera at infinity this reduces to 1 + z = (1 - r_g/R)^(-1/2) and I_nu,obs(nu) = (1+z)^(-3) I_nu,em((1+z)nu); far from the star it reduces to the special-relativistic Doppler factor.  
  src: `PRD` The shot, Frame; anchor: “shifts of the star and the sky follow from that one transformation.”
- **pipeline.gaunt-factor** [pipeline] — Thermally averaged free-free Gaunt factor from Coulomb wavefunctions. Compute the exact non-relativistic dipole free-free Gaunt factor g_ff(eta_i, eta_f) from Sommerfeld's hypergeometric closed form (Coulomb continuum wavefunctions), Maxwell-average it over the initial electron energy to get g-bar_ff(u = h nu / k_B T, gamma^2 = Z^2 Ry / k_B T) (dimensionless); the magnetic non-Born correction is applied downstream, not here.  
  src: `PRD` Milestones, 3; anchor: “audit and salvage the v1 atmosphere solver”
- **pipeline.mode-opacities** [pipeline] — Normal-mode absorption and scattering opacities. For each normal mode j (and pair j -> j' for scattering) at (nu, theta_kB, rho, T, B), project the cyclic-component free-free and scattering cross sections on the mode polarisation vectors to give kappa^abs_j and kappa^sc_jj' in cm^2 g^-1; at B = 0, kappa_abs,j = kappa_ff and sum over j' of kappa_sc,jj' = kappa_T (it is the thermal source intensity that is halved between modes, not each mode's total extinction); the angular dependence of scattering is an explicit approximation.  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “surface emission as spectral, angular, and polarised radiance from (a)”
- **pipeline.ns-exterior-spacetime** [pipeline] — Schwarzschild exterior of RX J1856. Given gravitational mass M (g) and circumferential radius R (cm), set up the static Schwarzschild exterior r >= R: r_g = 2GM/c^2, compactness u = r_g/R, lapse (1 - r_g/r)^(1/2), surface redshift 1 + z = (1 - u)^(-1/2), and the apparent quantities R_inf = R(1+z), T_inf = T/(1+z). Rotation and oblateness are neglected.  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “exact Schwarzschild geodesics from a finite-radius moving camera;”
- **pipeline.null-geodesic-trace** [pipeline] — Exact null geodesic from camera pixel to surface or sky. For a ray of impact parameter b (cm) starting at the camera radius r_c, integrate the exact Schwarzschild orbit equation (or evaluate the exact bending integral) in its orbital plane: decide hit (the past-directed ray reaches r = R before an exterior turning point or escape; an exterior turning point above R prevents a hit; the initial radial branch is retained; the surface-grazing b_max requires R > 3GM/c^2) or escape; on a hit return the surface point (theta, phi), the emission angle alpha (cos alpha relative to the local normal) and the azimuth of the photon direction relative to the local B; on escape return the asymptotic sky direction. Multiple images (bending > pi) are included.  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “exact Schwarzschild geodesics from a finite-radius moving camera;”
- **pipeline.pixel-radiance** [pipeline] — Pixel spectral radiance in the camera frame (unpolarised). For each pixel direction of the camera tetrad and each frequency nu_cam (Hz), trace the null geodesic backwards; if it hits the star, take the local surface radiance I^(j)_nu'(nu', mu, T_s, B) in the surface comoving frame and transform it with I_nu/nu^3 invariance to I_nu(nu_cam); if it escapes, take the sky radiance in the asymptotic direction and transform it the same way. Sum the polarisation modes into the unpolarised specific intensity I only, in the stated gravity-only transparent exterior (no Stokes Q, U, V: that needs basis transport, exterior vacuum polarisation evolution and phase averaging, which have no computation dependencies). Output in erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1 sr^-1, with a scale-adaptive switch to a point source plus PSF when the disc is unresolved.  
  src: `PRD` The shot, Primary output; anchor: “HDR spectral radiance per pixel in absolute units, with”
- **pipeline.rendered-frame** [pipeline] — Rendered frame (HDR radiance plus derived display image). Root of the spine. For one camera event (proper time tau on the camera worldline) produce (i) the HDR spectral radiance cube I_nu(x, y, nu) (unpolarised; no Q, U, V until polarised transport exists) in erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1 sr^-1 in the camera frame, and (ii) the display image (8-bit sRGB per pixel) derived from it through the stated colour, exposure and tone transforms. Milestone 1 delivers a single frame; the >= 60 s video needs milestone 4 and a separate time-remapping computation, not merely repeated frames. The Stokes Q, U, V content is limited to what pipeline.pixel-radiance supplies (unpolarised intensity only).  
  src: `PRD` Requirements, R8; anchor: “One 4k still at periastron, one video of at least 60 s, and the HDR radiance beh”
- **pipeline.scattering-opacity** [pipeline] — Electron and proton scattering cross sections. Cyclic-component electron and proton scattering cross sections sigma^sc_alpha(omega) (cm^2) in a magnetic field from the damped-oscillator (classical) form with radiative and collisional damping, electron scattering tending to sigma_T when damping is negligible and proton scattering retaining the (m_e/m_p)^2 suppression, with the region around the electron cyclotron resonance excluded from the undamped form, plus the angular redistribution (dipole/Rayleigh phase function) used by the transfer equation.  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “surface emission as spectral, angular, and polarised radiance from (a)”
- **pipeline.star-scale-adaptive** [pipeline] — Scale-adaptive star rendering (point source to resolved disc). When the star's apparent angular radius (from b_max and the camera radius) is smaller than a pixel, replace ray sampling by the total spectral flux F_nu = integral I_nu dOmega over the image plane (erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1), deposited through the camera PSF; when resolved, sample the disc with enough rays per pixel to resolve the limb and the lensed ring; blend across the transition so that total flux is conserved. Finite-camera solid angle: integrate over the camera-frame image plane using gr.observer-sky-angle (not the distant-observer image-plane element); the PSF is unit-normalised. gr.disk-angular-radius and gr.image-plane-solid-angle are distant-static verification targets only (their sources take the distant-observer limit).  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “scale-adaptive star rendering (point with PSF to resolved disc);”
- **pipeline.surface-maps-temperature** [pipeline] — Surface temperature map T_s(theta, phi). Compute the local effective surface temperature T_s (K) at each surface point. Milestone 1: uniform T_s (single T_eff). Milestone 3: T_s from the field geometry by anisotropic heat conduction through the magnetised envelope, either the GH83 anisotropic-slab distribution or the PPP15 Appendix-B fit (stubs) and finally our own envelope solve (pipeline.envelope-tb-ts), with the overall T_eff defined by T_eff^4 = (4 pi R^2)^(-1) integral T_s^4 dSigma; constrained by the observed pulse amplitude.  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “constrained by the observed pulse”
- **pipeline.surface-parameters** [pipeline] — RX J1856 star parameters (M, R, T, B, geometry, N_H). Provide the labelled parameter set for a render: M (g), R (cm) or (z, R_inf), T_b or T_eff (K), B_pole (G), magnetic obliquity and viewing geometry, envelope composition and N_H (cm^-2), at d = 123 pc. Milestone 1: an ensemble input labelled by provenance (Ho+2007 thin-atmosphere output, or the Chandra X-ray blackbody kT_inf and R_inf/d). Milestone 2-3: our own maximum-likelihood fit of these parameters to the HST photometry, the X-ray spectrum and the pulse amplitude, with that inference a separate computation (pipeline.earth-photometry is its forward model but is NOT a dependency here, which would create a cycle); here the parameters are labelled trial values. The Ho+2007 radius is quoted for 140 pc and must not be reused unchanged at 123 pc. The spin-down field is distinct from B_pole.  
  src: `PRD` Success criteria; anchor: “The surface-state uncertainty is presented”
- **pipeline.surface-radiance** [pipeline] — Surface radiance interface (three interchangeable models). At a surface point (theta, phi) with local T_s (K), B vector (G) and field-normal angle Theta, return the emergent specific intensity in the surface rest frame for each normal mode j = X, O (or Stokes I, Q, U, V), I^(j)_nu(nu, cos alpha, azimuth) in erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1 sr^-1, from one of three models behind one interface, given explicit model inputs: surface gravity g (cm s^-2), hydrogen column (g cm^-2), substrate composition and boundary state (T_s and B alone do not select a solution); output Stokes parameters are phase-averaged (stated; the conversion requires a phase treatment). Branches: blackbody (milestone 1), atmosphere models (milestone 3): blackbody, hydrogen atmosphere, thin hydrogen layer over a condensed surface.  
  src: `PRD` Requirements, R4; anchor: “models are interchangeable behind one interface”
- **pipeline.surface-radiance-blackbody** [pipeline] — Blackbody surface radiance. Isotropic, unpolarised Planck intensity B_nu(T_s) = (2 h nu^3 / c^2) / (exp(h nu / k_B T_s) - 1) in erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1 sr^-1 at the local T_s, split equally between the two modes; no colour correction and no limb darkening (f_col = 1, p = 0 by definition).  
  src: `PRD` Milestones, 1; anchor: “1. Spacetime, camera, blackbody disc, real sky. First honest image.”
- **pipeline.surface-radiance-h-atmosphere** [pipeline] — Hydrogen-atmosphere surface radiance. Emergent two-mode specific intensity I^(j)_nu(nu, mu, azimuth) (erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1 sr^-1) of a fully ionised hydrogen atmosphere (an intermediate approximation: the Ho 2007 RX J1856 comparison requires partial ionisation) in radiative and hydrostatic equilibrium at local (T_eff = T_s, g, B, Theta), obtained by a formal solution at the requested nu and mu on the converged atmosphere structure; B = 0 reduces to the McPHAC single-mode case.  
  src: `PRD` Milestones, 3; anchor: “3. Surface models: audit and salvage the v1 atmosphere solver; add the”
- **pipeline.vacuum-mode-conversion** [pipeline] — Vacuum resonance and partial mode conversion. Locate the vacuum resonance density rho_V (g cm^-3) where plasma and vacuum contributions to the mode parameter cancel (root find on our own tensor), compute the adiabaticity energy E_ad (keV) from the density scale height H_rho = |ds/d ln rho| measured along the ray at resonance (low-energy, isolated-resonance conditions apply) and the non-adiabatic jump probability P_jump = exp[-(pi/2)(E/E_ad)^3], and apply the resulting partial X <-> O conversion inside the two-mode transfer at the resonance depth.  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “surface emission as spectral, angular, and polarised radiance from (a)”
- **pipeline.vacuum-polarisation** [pipeline] — QED vacuum-polarisation coefficients. Compute the vacuum dielectric and permeability corrections a-hat(b), q(b), m(b) (dimensionless, b = B/B_Q) from the one-loop Euler-Heisenberg (Heyl-Hernquist) closed form at arbitrary field, checked against the weak-field limit a-hat = -2 alpha_f b^2/(45 pi), q = 7 alpha_f b^2/(45 pi), m = -4 alpha_f b^2/(45 pi); valid for h nu << m_e c^2.  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “surface emission as spectral, angular, and polarised radiance from (a)”

## rt

- **rt.adiabatic-energy-val** [equation] — Adiabatic energy for resonant conversion (VAL06). Lai & Ho (2002): a photon undergoes resonant mode conversion when E is greater than about E_ad, with E_ad depending on the field-photon angle, the ion cyclotron energy and the density scale height along the ray.  
  `E_{ad} = 2.52\left[f_B\tan\theta_{kB}\left|1-(E_{Bi}/E)^2\right|\right]^{2/3}\left(\frac{1\ \mathrm{cm}}{H_\rho}\right)^{1/3}`  
  src: `van_adelsberg_lai_2006_magnetic_atm` eq. 3; anchor: “undergoes resonant mode conversion when the adiabatic”
- **rt.airy-first-zero** [equation] — First zero of the Airy pattern, 1.22 lambda/D. The first minimum of the Airy function is found at 1.22 lambda/D, where lambda is the wavelength and D the aperture diameter. Derivation from Eqs. 4-5 (rt.airy-intensity-pattern): with x_psf = pi D_ap theta_psf/lambda, the pattern vanishes where J_1(x_psf) = 0 and x_psf != 0, so the first minimum is at x_1, the first positive root of J_1, giving theta_{1,psf} = (x_{1,psf}/pi) lambda/D_ap, and x_{1,psf}/pi = 1.21966989... is approximately 1.22 (the paper's three-digit rounding).  
  `\theta_{1,psf} = \frac{x_{1,psf}}{\pi}\,\frac{\lambda}{D_{ap}} \simeq 1.22\,\frac{\lambda}{D_{ap}}, \qquad \mathrm{J}_1(x_{1,psf}) = 0,\ x_{1,psf} = 3.8317059702\ \text{(first positive root)}`  
  src: `norton_2025_hmi_stray_light` Sec. 2.1, after eqs. 4-5; anchor: “The first minimum of the Airy function is found at 1.22”
- **rt.airy-intensity-pattern** [equation] — Airy diffraction pattern of a circular aperture (normalised PSF). The intensity PSF of an ideal incoherent imaging system with a circular aperture of diameter D_ap, focal length f_foc and wavelength lambda is the Airy function PSF(r') = (2 J_1(r')/r')^2 (normalised to 1 at the centre) with r' = pi D_ap r_fp/(f_foc lambda), r_fp being the radial distance in the focal plane. Under the paraxial substitution r_fp = f_foc theta_psf (theta_psf the small angle off the optical axis) this is I_psf(theta_psf) = I_peak [2 J_1(x_psf)/x_psf]^2 with x_psf = pi D_ap theta_psf/lambda, I_peak the central intensity.  
  `I_{psf}(\theta_{psf}) = I_{peak} \left[\frac{2 \mathrm{J}_1(x_{psf})}{x_{psf}}\right]^2, \qquad x_{psf} = \frac{\pi D_{ap}\,\theta_{psf}}{\lambda}`  
  src: `norton_2025_hmi_stray_light` Sec. 2.1, eqs. 4-5; anchor: “the intensity of the ideal PSF can be described as an Airy function which is pro”
- **rt.approx-coherent-scattering-mcphac** [approximation] — Coherent (non-Compton) scattering (McPHAC). Scattering is treated as coherent. Because of this the radiative transfer equation is solved one frequency at a time with no direct frequency coupling; the paper notes this could cause inaccuracies at energies above 5 keV (1 percent of the electron rest mass).  
  src: `haakonsen_2012_mcphac` Sect. 2, assumption 2 (p. 3); Sect. 3.3; anchor: “coherent scattering is assumed, which could lead to inac-”
- **rt.approx-no-radiation-pressure-mcphac** [approximation] — Radiation pressure neglected (McPHAC). Radiation pressure is neglected so that the pressure at any depth equals the weight of the overlying column; the paper says this is appropriate for atmospheres with T_eff much less than 1e7 K.  
  src: `haakonsen_2012_mcphac` Sect. 2, assumption 7 (p. 3); anchor: “radiation pressure is neglected, which is appropriate for”
- **rt.approx-plane-parallel-mcphac** [approximation] — Plane-parallel atmosphere (McPHAC). The plane-parallel assumption is used since the scale height of the atmosphere is much smaller than the neutron-star radius; surface gravity is taken uniform because a negligible fraction of the star mass lies in the atmosphere.  
  src: `haakonsen_2012_mcphac` Sect. 2, assumption 6 (p. 3); anchor: “the plane-parallel assumption is used, since the scale height”
- **rt.boundary-conditions-mcphac** [equation] — Transfer-equation boundary conditions (McPHAC). Zero incident specific intensity at the surface (so P_nu is half the outgoing intensity there) and P_nu equal to the blackbody intensity B_nu at the deepest point considered; the bottom condition is a second-order accurate approximation to the diffusion boundary condition and ensures isotropic intensity at the bottom depth.  
  `I_\nu(0,-\mu) = 0 \;(I^- = 0), \qquad P_\nu(y_{\max},\mu) = B_\nu`  
  src: `haakonsen_2012_mcphac` Sect. 2 (p. 3) and Sect. 3.3 (p. 5); anchor: “The boundary conditions used are zero in-”
- **rt.boundary-conditions-spw09** [equation] — Outer and inner boundary conditions, two modes (SPW09). No external radiation at the outer boundary (incoming rays vanish at m_1) and the diffusion approximation at the inner boundary, with each mode carrying B_nu/2 for outgoing rays at m_max.  
  `I_\nu^i(\mu<0,\,m=m_1)=0, \qquad I_\nu^i(\mu>0,\,m=m_{\max}) = \frac{B_\nu}{2}`  
  src: `suleimanov_potekhin_werner_2009_mag_atm` eqs. 14-15; anchor: “We use the conventional condition (no external radiation) at”
- **rt.boundary-conditions-val** [equation] — Boundary conditions for integrating the mode equations (VAL06). Upward and downward integration of the mode transfer equation starts from the thermalised deep boundary (Planck/2 for outgoing rays) and zero incident intensity at the outer edge; tau_max and tau_min are chosen to span 5-8 orders of magnitude.  
  `I_\nu^j(\tau\to\tau_{\max},+\mu)\to B_\nu/2, \qquad I_\nu^j(\tau\to\tau_{\min},-\mu)\to 0`  
  src: `van_adelsberg_lai_2006_magnetic_atm` eqs. 35-36; anchor: “Iνj (τ → τmax , +µ)      →   Bν /2”
- **rt.cond-approx-bc-truncation** [approximation] — Truncation of fitted mode reflectivities to 0 < R_MM' < 1. Because the fit error may exceed 1 - R_XX when the X-mode is almost completely reflected (E_ci < E < E_C with k and B near normal), the fitting formulae can give R_XX a few percent above 1 at very small theta_B and theta_k; the mode-specific reflectivities recovered from the fit must then be truncated so that 0 < R_MM' < 1.  
  src: `potekhin_2012_condensed_surface` sect. B.1 (p. 14); anchor: “truncate the mode-specific reflectivities, recovered”
- **rt.cond-approx-bc-vacuum-interface** [approximation] — Reflection at atmosphere-condensed interface replaced by vacuum values. Strictly the reflection coefficients r_mj at the interface between the thin atmosphere and the condensed surface differ from those with vacuum above the surface and would require a separate calculation for each atmosphere. For a sufficiently rarefied atmosphere they are approximately replaced by the vacuum coefficients; the plane waves are then almost transverse, so K_z,M -> 0 in eq. 4 and each wave is expanded over the linear polarisation vectors e_1, e_2.  
  src: `potekhin_2012_condensed_surface` sect. B.1 (p. 13); anchor: “approximately replace these coefficients by those in vac-”
- **rt.cond-approx-condensation-condition** [approximation] — Condition for a bare condensed surface (negligible vapour). A smooth condensed metallic surface with negligible vapour above it is assumed when T is at least a few times below T_crit; for H, van Adelsberg+ state there is no question that the surface is condensed for T <~ T_crit/2. Near T ~ T_crit the surface is hidden by an optically thick atmosphere, and for T << T_crit the atmosphere becomes optically thin (Potekhin+ 2012, p. 3), so intermediate cases need a thin atmosphere on the condensed surface.

- **rt.cond-approx-damping-low-energy** [approximation] — Damping from the zero-frequency conductivity at E <~ E_pe. For E >> E_pe electron-ion collisions are treated as independent (free-free rates of one electron-ion pair); this fails for E <~ E_pe where collective effects matter and electron degeneracy is important, so gamma_ei is approximated there by the zero-frequency conductivity result of Potekhin (1999). That calculation neglects the effect of B on ion motion and so applies only for u_i -> 0 (fixed-ion limit) or E >> E_Bi; the emissivity at E <~ E_Bi is insensitive to the damping rates.  
  src: `van_adelsberg_2005_condensed_surface` sect. 2.3 (p. 4); anchor: “The calculations of νei and νei adopted in our paper”
- **rt.cond-approx-fixed-ions** [approximation] — Fixed-ion limit of the ion response in the condensed matter. Ion motion is neglected altogether (ion mass m_i = infinity, equivalently u_i -> 0 or E_ci -> 0 in the fit formulae), as implicitly adopted by Brinkmann (1980) and Turolla+ (2004). The reflectivity then shows no sharp change at E_ci and continues smoothly to lower energies, where J is lower than in the free-ion case.

- **rt.cond-approx-free-ions** [approximation] — Free-ion limit of the ion response in the condensed matter. Ions respond to the electromagnetic wave as free (quasi-free) particles in the magnetic field, neglecting Coulomb interactions between ions, i.e. the full dielectric tensor of van Adelsberg et al. (2005), eqs. 2-3 with u_i retained. The reflectivity then has sharp structure at E = E_ci, and a broad suppression of J between E_ci and E_C. The actual surface spectrum is expected to lie between the free-ion and fixed-ion limits.  
  src: `potekhin_2012_condensed_surface` sect. 1 (p. 1-2) and sect. 2.2.3 (p. 4); anchor: “neglecting the Coulomb interactions between”
- **rt.cond-approx-no-vacuum-polarisation** [approximation] — Vacuum polarisation neglected in condensed-surface reflectivity. The vacuum-polarisation effect is neglected in the mode equation of the condensed medium because its density is far above the vacuum-resonance density rho_V ~ 0.96 (A/Z) B14^2 (E/keV)^2 g cm^-3; outside the surface the vacuum dielectric and permeability tensors differ negligibly from unity (|q|, |m| << 1) for B << 5e16 G.  
  src: `van_adelsberg_2005_condensed_surface` footnote 8 and sect. 3.2 (p. 5); anchor: “vacuum resonance density, ρV ≃”
- **rt.cond-approx-planar-patch** [approximation] — Smooth planar surface patch. The emitting surface element is taken small enough that variations of the magnetic field strength and inclination are negligible, and is treated as a plane, neglecting its curvature and roughness.

- **rt.cond-bc-mode-reflection** [equation] — Normal-mode reflectivities R_MM' from the r_mj amplitudes, Potekhin 2012 eqs. B.5-B.7. For a sufficiently rarefied atmosphere, with nearly transverse waves, the normal-mode reflectivities used in the atmosphere boundary condition are R_MM' = |r'_MM'|^2, where the reflected-mode amplitudes r'_XM' and r'_OM' (M' = X, O) solve the 2x2 linear system obtained by expanding the incident mode polarisation vector e_M' = c^(i)_M'1 e_1 + c^(i)_M'2 e_2 (eq. B.4) over the linear polarisation basis, sum_M r'_MM' e_M^(r) = sum_{m,j} r_mj c^(i)_M'j e_m^(r) (eq. B.5); the scalar products c_Mj use K_M(alpha_i,r) from eq. 4 with K_z,M -> 0 (eqs. B.8-B.12). The incident X- and O-modes are incoherent.

- **rt.cond-dielectric-tensor-condensed** [equation] — Cold-plasma dielectric tensor of the condensed matter, van Adelsberg 2005 eqs. 2-3. In the free-electron-gas model with B along z the dielectric tensor is [[eps, i g, 0], [-i g, eps, 0], [0, 0, eta]] with eps +/- g ≃ 1 - v_e/[(1 +/- u_e^(1/2))(1 -/+ u_i^(1/2)) + i gamma_ei^(tr)] and eta ≃ 1 - v_e/(1 + i gamma_ei^(l)), where u_e = (E_Be/E)^2, u_i = (E_Bi/E)^2, v_e = (E_pe/E)^2 and gamma = hbar nu_ei/E are the dimensionless collisional damping rates. - **rt.cond-inner-bc** [equation] — Inner boundary condition of a thin atmosphere on a condensed surface, Potekhin 2012 eqs. 29-30. Below E_ci the free-ion and fixed-ion reflectivities differ sharply.

- **rt.cond-kirchhoff-law** [equation] — Kirchhoff emission of a macroscopic body, van Adelsberg 2005 eqs. 7-8. Placing the body in an unpolarised blackbody cavity at its own temperature and requiring the cavity field to stay unpolarised gives the intrinsic emission in each reflected polarisation, I_nu,j^(e) = B_nu/2 - I_nu,j^(r) = (1 - R_j) B_nu/2, so that the total emission is I_nu^(e) = (1 - R) B_nu(T) = J B_nu(T) with R = (R_1 + R_2)/2 the reflectivity and J = 1 - R the dimensionless emissivity; these hold also out of equilibrium since they are intrinsic properties of the body.  
  `I^{(e)}_{\nu j} = \tfrac12 B_\nu - I^{(r)}_{\nu j} = \tfrac12 (1-R_j) B_\nu,\qquad I^{(e)}_\nu = (1-R)\,B_\nu(T) \equiv J B_\nu(T)`  
  src: `van_adelsberg_2005_condensed_surface` eqs. 7a, 7b, 8 (p. 4-5); anchor: “Iν(e) = (1 − R)Bν (T ) ≡ JBν (T )”
- **rt.cond-linear-polarisation-degree** [equation] — Degree of linear polarisation of condensed-surface emission, Potekhin 2012 eq. 28. The degree of linear polarisation of the emitted radiation is P_lin = (J_1 - J_2)/(2J) = (R_2 - R_1)/(2 - 2R). Both papers use the same algebraic expression in their respective bases; P_lin > 0 means J_1 > J_2.  
  `P_{\rm lin} = (J_1 - J_2)/2J = (R_2 - R_1)/(2 - 2R)`  
  src: `potekhin_2012_condensed_surface` eq. 28 (p. 7); anchor: “Plin = (J1 − J2 )/2J = (R2 − R1 )/(2 − 2R).”
- **rt.cond-reflectivity-from-amplitudes** [equation] — Effective mode reflectivity from reflected-wave amplitudes, Potekhin 2012 eq. A.2. A linearly polarised incident wave E_j^(i) = A_j e_j^(i) produces reflected field E_j^(r) = A_j sum_m r_mj e_m^(r) and transmitted field E_j^(t) = A_j sum_m t_mj e_m^(t) (eq. A.1); the effective reflectivity of reflected polarisation j under unpolarised incidence is R_j = |r_j1|^2 + |r_j2|^2 with J_j = 1 - R_j.  
  `R_j = |r_{j1}|^2 + |r_{j2}|^2\quad (j=1,2)`  
  src: `potekhin_2012_condensed_surface` eqs. A.1-A.2 (p. 12); anchor: “R j = |r j1 |2 + |r j2 |2   ( j = 1, 2).”
- **rt.cond-reflectivity-regimes** [result] — Characteristic energy ranges of the free-ion reflectivity. For free ions the reflectivity of the condensed surface behaves differently in three ranges, E < E_ci, E_ci <= E <~ E_C and E >~ E_C, with an additional suppression of the emissivity near E ~ E_pe whose position, width and depth depend on theta_B, theta_k and phi. For fixed ions the reflectivity is similar at E > E_ci but without the sharp change at E_ci.  
  src: `potekhin_2012_condensed_surface` sect. 2.2.3 (p. 4); Sect. 2.3.1, eq. 21, p. 5; anchor: “Finally, the lowering of J(E) at E > ẼC is fit by”
- **rt.cond-surface-density** [equation] — Order-of-magnitude surface density of the condensed phase, Potekhin 2012 eq. 2. The density of the condensed surface layer is estimated as rho_s = 8.9e3 eta A Z^-0.6 B13^1.2 g cm^-3, where A, Z are the atomic mass and charge numbers and eta ~ 1 is an unknown factor absorbing the theoretical uncertainty; eta = 1 is the ion-sphere (Salpeter 1954) equation of state. The density enters the reflectivity through E_pe and the weakly dependent damping.  
  `\rho_s = 8.9\times10^{3}\,\eta\,A Z^{-0.6} B_{13}^{1.2}\ {\rm g\,cm^{-3}}`

- **rt.cond-tcrit-fit-fe** [result] — Critical temperature for magnetic condensation of Fe, Potekhin 2012 p. 3. Medin & Lai (2007), from DFT cohesive energies Q_s and saturated-vapour densities, found T_crit ~ 0.08 Q_s/k_B, with numerical results for 56Fe at 0.5 <= B13 <= 100 described by T_crit ~ (5 + 2 B13) x 1e5 K (and eta ~ 0.55 in the surface-density eq. 2), with uncertainties below 20% for both quantities. - **rt.eddington-factors-mcphac** [definition] — Eddington factors and mean intensity (McPHAC). Eddington factor f_nu is the second angular moment of P_nu normalised by the mean intensity J_nu; h_nu is the first moment normalised by J_nu, used at the surface boundary condition of the temperature correction.

In the Eddington approximation the temperature profile satisfies a differential equation in column depth involving the Rosseland mean opacity; integrated from the surface with T(0) = 0.265 T_eff it gives the initial guess for the iteration.

The angle integral in the source function is replaced by a Gauss-Legendre sum with weights a_j, and the transfer equation is rewritten with total opacity k_nu and albedo rho_nu using d tau_nu = k_nu dy.  
  `\int_0^1 P_\nu(y,\mu^\prime)\frac{d\sigma_{T,r}}{d\mu^\prime}(\mu,\mu^\prime)d\mu^\prime \approx \sum_{j^\prime=1}^{M} P_\nu(y,\mu_{j^\prime})\frac{d\sigma_{T,r}}{d\mu^\prime}(\mu,\mu_{j^\prime})a_{j^\prime}, \qquad \frac{\mu^2}{k_\nu}\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac{1}{k_\nu}\frac{dP_\nu(y,\mu)}{dy}\right) = P_\nu(y,\mu) - (1-\rho_\nu)B_\nu(T(y)) - \frac{2\rho_\nu}{\sigma_{T,r}}\sum_{j^\prime=1}^{M} P_\nu(y,\mu_{j^\prime})\frac{d\sigma_{T,r}}{d\mu^\prime}(\mu,\mu_{j^\prime})a_{j^\prime}`

- **rt.feautrier-second-order-mcphac** [equation] — Feautrier second-order transfer equation (McPHAC). Second-order form of the radiative transfer equation in the Feautrier variable P_nu = (I(mu)+I(-mu))/2, with effective normal optical depth tau_nu and source function S_nu.  
  `\mu^2 \frac{d^2 P_\nu(y,\mu)}{d\tau_\nu^2} = P_\nu(y,\mu) - S_\nu(y,\mu), \qquad P_\nu(y,\mu) \equiv \tfrac{1}{2}\left[I_\nu(y,\mu)+I_\nu(y,-\mu)\right]`

- **rt.flux-constancy-mcphac** [equation] — Radiative equilibrium: flux independent of depth (McPHAC App. A). Integrating the second-order transfer equation over mu and over frequency gives that the divergence of the total flux equals the integral of (J_nu - B_nu) kappa_nu; in radiative equilibrium the energy flux is the same at every depth, so the right-hand side vanishes.  
  `\frac{1}{4\pi}\frac{d}{dy}\int_0^\infty F_\nu\,d\nu = \int_0^\infty (J_\nu - B_\nu(T(y)))\kappa_\nu\,d\nu = 0, \qquad F_\nu = \frac{4\pi}{k_\nu}\frac{d}{dy}(f_\nu J_\nu)`

- **rt.flux-constraints-val** [equation] — Radiative equilibrium and constant flux constraints (VAL06). The transfer equation is solved subject to radiative equilibrium (frequency-integrated absorption equals emission, summed over modes) and a constant radiative flux equal to sigma_sb T_eff^4.

- **rt.hydrostatic-column-mcphac** [equation] — Hydrostatic equilibrium in column depth (McPHAC). With radiation pressure neglected, the pressure at any depth equals the weight of the integrated column y of material above it, with uniform surface gravity g_s.  
  `P(y) = g_s\, y`

- **rt.hydrostatic-spw09** [equation] — Hydrostatic equilibrium with radiation pressure (SPW09). Hydrostatic equilibrium in column density m including radiative acceleration, with surface gravity from the exterior Schwarzschild metric, and the definition of column density.  
  `\frac{dP_g}{dm} = g - g_{\rm rad}, \quad g = \frac{GM_{\rm NS}}{R_{\rm NS}^2\sqrt{1-R_S/R_{\rm NS}}}, \quad g_{\rm rad} = \frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\int_0^\infty d\nu\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi\int_{-1}^{+1}(k_\nu^i+\sigma_\nu^i)\,\mu\,I_\nu^i(\mu,\varphi)\,d\mu, \quad dm = -\rho\,dz`

- **rt.mode-stokes-relations-val** [equation] — Mode intensities from Stokes parameters and back (VAL06). Away from the vacuum resonance, neglecting dissipative terms in the dielectric tensor, the mode intensities follow from Stokes I, Q, V and the mixing angle theta_m; conversely the Stokes parameters follow from the mode intensities with a random phase difference Delta phi between the modes, so Q, U, V need phase sampling while the mode intensities do not.  
  `I_\nu^{\pm} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[I_\nu \pm (\cos2\theta_m Q_\nu+\sin2\theta_m V_\nu)\right], \quad I_\nu = I_\nu^{+}+I_\nu^{-}, \quad Q_\nu = \cos2\theta_m(I_\nu^{+}-I_\nu^{-}) - 2\sin2\theta_m(I_\nu^{+}I_\nu^{-})^{1/2}\cos\Delta\phi, \quad U_\nu = -2(I_\nu^{+}I_\nu^{-})^{1/2}\sin\Delta\phi, \quad V_\nu = \sin2\theta_m(I_\nu^{+}-I_\nu^{-}) + 2\cos2\theta_m(I_\nu^{+}I_\nu^{-})^{1/2}\cos\Delta\phi`

- **rt.no-feautrier-with-conversion-val** [approximation] — Standard Feautrier substitution not used for VAL06 partial conversion. - **rt.observed-flux-redshift-mcphac** [equation] — Observed flux from emergent flux with redshift (McPHAC). For a neutron star with homogeneous surface temperature the flux observed at distance D follows from the emergent flux at the stellar surface radius R, evaluated at the blueshifted frequency, with the Schwarzschild redshift factor 1+z.  
  `F(D,\nu_{\rm obs}) = (1+z)^{-1}\frac{R^2}{D^2}F\left(R,(1+z)\nu_{\rm obs}\right), \qquad 1+z = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{Rc^2}}}`

- **rt.pjump-conversion-spw09** [equation] — Partial mode conversion at the vacuum resonance (SPW09). At the vacuum resonance the extraordinary-mode intensity converts partially into the ordinary mode with probability 1 - P_jump and vice versa; P_jump is an exponential function of (E/E_ad)^3, where E_ad depends on E, B, rho, T, mu.  
  `I_\nu^{1,2}\rightarrow P_{\rm jump}I_\nu^{1,2}+(1-P_{\rm jump})I_\nu^{2,1}, \qquad P_{\rm jump} = \exp\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}(E/E_{\rm ad})^3\right]`  
  src: `suleimanov_potekhin_werner_2009_mag_atm` eqs. 16-17; anchor: “Iν1,2 → Pjump Iν1,2 + (1 − Pjump ) Iν2,1 ,                       (16)”
- **rt.pjump-val** [equation] — Non-adiabatic jump probability and mode conversion rule (VAL06). With probability 1 - P_jump an O-mode photon converts to X-mode (and vice versa) at the vacuum resonance; P_jump is the non-adiabatic jump probability. Intensities are exchanged across the resonance accordingly. Complete conversion is P_jump = 0 and no conversion is P_jump = 1.  
  `P_{\rm jump} = \exp\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}(E/E_{ad})^3\right], \qquad I_X \to P_{\rm jump}I_X+(1-P_{\rm jump})I_O, \qquad I_O \to P_{\rm jump}I_O+(1-P_{\rm jump})I_X`  
  src: `van_adelsberg_lai_2006_magnetic_atm` eqs. 4, 33-34; anchor: “Pjump = exp − (E/Ead )3 .”
- **rt.planck-function-blambda** [equation] — Planck function B_lambda(T) (per unit wavelength). Power emitted per unit area per steradian per unit wavelength interval by a blackbody: B_lambda = (2 h c^2 / lambda^5) / (exp[h c / (lambda k T)] - 1). B_lambda and B_nu are different functions of different variables related by B_lambda |d lambda| = B_nu |d nu| (equal power in corresponding spectral ranges; eqs. 5-6 reverse the integration limits and use absolute differentials), not by substituting lambda = c/nu.  
  `B_\lambda =\frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5}\frac{1}{\exp[hc/(\lambda kT)]-1}`  
  src: `marr_2011_planck_law` eq. 1 and eq. 5; anchor: “where h and k are the Planck and Boltzmann constants and c is the speed of light”
- **rt.planck-function-bnu** [equation] — Planck function B_nu(T) (per unit frequency). Power emitted per unit area per steradian per unit frequency interval by a blackbody at temperature T, as a function of frequency nu: B_nu = (2 h nu^3 / c^2) / (exp[h nu / (k T)] - 1), with h the Planck constant, k the Boltzmann constant, c the speed of light. In Gaussian CGS B_nu has units erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1 sr^-1.  
  `B_\nu =\frac{2h\nu^3}{c^2}\frac{1}{\exp[h\nu/(kT)]-1}`  
  src: `marr_2011_planck_law` eq. 2; anchor: “emitted power per unit area per steradian per frequency interval.”
- **rt.planck-integral-stefan-boltzmann** [equation] — Integral of B_nu over frequency equals sigma T^4 / pi. A blackbody radiates, per unit area per steradian across the whole spectrum, sigma T^4 / pi, with sigma the Stefan-Boltzmann constant; the formula is obtained by integrating B_nu over all frequencies from zero to infinity. The 1/pi appears because the Stefan-Boltzmann law is the integral of intensity over solid angle.  
  `\int_{0}^{\infty}{B_\nu \,d\nu} = {\sigma T^4 \over \pi}`  
  src: `marr_2011_planck_law` eq. 9; anchor: “frequencies, from zero to infinity, that is,”
- **rt.psf-aperture-convention** [pipeline] — Airy PSF for point-source and unresolved-star rendering (project convention). Project convention: the renderer convolves every unresolved source (point-source background stars and the unresolved neutron star) with the unit-integral Airy kernel K_{psf} = 1_S A_{psf} / integral over S of A_{psf} dOmega, on a logged support S restricted to the paraxial regime, with K_{psf} = 0 outside S, where A_{psf} = [2 J_1(x_psf)/x_psf]^2 is the peak-normalised pattern of rt.airy-intensity-pattern (A_{psf} = 1 at the centre) for a stated circular aperture diameter D_ap. The printed A_{psf} is peak-normalised, not unit-normalised; the unit-integral normalisation is the division by its integral. The support S and any truncation within it are logged. D_ap and the wavelength sampling used for x_psf = pi D_ap theta_psf/lambda are logged parameters of every rendered frame. The per-wavelength PSF is the primary option; evaluating at a single stated effective wavelength is an approximation and is logged. Total flux is conserved by the unit-integral normalisation.  
  `K_{psf} = \frac{A_{psf}}{\int A_{psf}\,d\Omega}, \qquad A_{psf} = \left[\frac{2\mathrm{J}_1(x_{psf})}{x_{psf}}\right]^2,\ x_{psf} = \frac{\pi D_{ap}\theta_{psf}}{\lambda}`  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “scale-adaptive star rendering (point with PSF to resolved disc);”
- **rt.source-function-mcphac** [equation] — Source function with anisotropic Thomson scattering (McPHAC). Source function as thermal emission weighted by absorption fraction plus scattered intensity weighted by the scattering fraction; scattering is not assumed isotropic. The scattering albedo is rho_nu = sigma_T,r/(kappa_nu+sigma_T,r) = sigma_T,r/k_nu.  
  `S_\nu(y,\mu) = \frac{\kappa_\nu}{\kappa_\nu+\sigma_{T,r}} B_\nu(T(y)) + \frac{2}{\kappa_\nu+\sigma_{T,r}}\int_0^1 P_\nu(y,\mu^\prime)\frac{d\sigma_{T,r}}{d\mu^\prime}(\mu,\mu^\prime)\,d\mu^\prime, \qquad \rho_\nu = \frac{\sigma_{T,r}}{\kappa_\nu+\sigma_{T,r}} = \frac{\sigma_{T,r}}{k_\nu}`

- **rt.surface-flux-spw09** [equation] — Surface flux condition and Eddington flux (SPW09). The emergent Eddington flux integrated over frequency must satisfy the effective-temperature condition at m=0; the Eddington flux is the mu-weighted angular integral of the mode intensities; the relative flux error is used as a convergence diagnostic.  
  `4\pi\int_0^\infty H_\nu(m=0)\,d\nu = \sigma T_{\rm eff}^4 = 4\pi H_0, \quad H_\nu(m) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi\int_{-1}^{+1}\mu\,I_\nu^i(\mu,\varphi,m)\,d\mu, \quad \varepsilon_H(m) = 1 - \frac{H_0}{\int_0^\infty H_\nu(m)\,d\nu}`

- **rt.te-delta-t-mcphac** [equation] — Linearised temperature correction enforcing constant flux (McPHAC App. A). Expanding the Planck function to first order about the current temperature profile and requiring the frequency-integrated energy balance gives the temperature correction DeltaT; the correction satisfies constant energy flux through the atmosphere.  
  `\Delta T = \frac{\int_0^\infty (J_\nu - B_\nu(T_0))\kappa_\nu\,d\nu}{\int_0^\infty \frac{dB_\nu}{dT}\kappa_\nu\,d\nu}`

- **rt.te-moment-equation-mcphac** [equation] — Moment equation and boundary conditions for the temperature correction (McPHAC). With the Eddington factor f_nu frozen from the full angular solution, J_nu is found from a one-dimensional moment equation (the transfer equation integrated over mu with the Taylor-expanded Planck function); at the top boundary d(f J)/(k dy) = h J, and at the bottom J_nu = B_nu.  
  `\frac{1}{k_\nu}\frac{d}{dy}\left[\frac{1}{k_\nu}\frac{d}{dy}(f_\nu J_\nu)\right] = \left[J_\nu - B_\nu(T_0) - \frac{dB_\nu}{dT}\frac{\int_0^\infty (J_\nu - B_\nu(T_0))\kappa_\nu d\nu}{\int_0^\infty \frac{dB_\nu}{dT}\kappa_\nu d\nu}\right](1-\rho_\nu), \qquad \frac{1}{k_\nu}\frac{d}{dy}(f_\nu J_\nu) = h_\nu J_\nu \;(\text{top}), \qquad J_\nu = B_\nu \;(\text{bottom})`  
  src: `haakonsen_2012_mcphac` eqs. A6, A26–A27; anchor: “To solve this equation, the fν computed by solving the full”
- **rt.te-rybicki-matrices-mcphac** [equation] — Rybicki-form discretised temperature-correction system (McPHAC App. A). The discretised moment equation is Ai J_{i-1} + Bi J_i + Ci J_{i+1} = Qi on K frequencies; restructured with the Rybicki method into tridiagonal matrices T_k per frequency plus a coupling U_k through the weighted-mean vector Jbar, with explicit interior-row elements for 1 < i < N_temp.  
  `\Delta_1 = [k_\nu(y_i)+k_\nu(y_{i-1})](y_i-y_{i-1}),\ \Delta_2 = [k_\nu(y_{i+1})+k_\nu(y_i)](y_{i+1}-y_i),\ \pi = \Delta_1+\Delta_2;\quad (\bar J)_i = \frac{\sum_{k^\prime}J_{k^\prime}\kappa_{k^\prime}b_{k^\prime}}{\sum_{k^\prime}\frac{dB_{k^\prime}}{dT}\kappa_{k^\prime}b_{k^\prime}};\quad \mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{J}_k+\mathbf{U}_k\bar{\mathbf{J}}=\mathbf{K}_k;\quad (T_k)_{i,i-1} = -\frac{8f_k(y_{i-1})}{\pi\Delta_1},\ (T_k)_{i,i+1} = -\frac{8f_k(y_{i+1})}{\pi\Delta_2},\ (T_k)_{i,i} = \left[\frac{1-\rho_k}{f_k(y_i)}+\frac{8}{\pi\Delta_1}+\frac{8}{\pi\Delta_2}\right]f_k(y_i),\ (U_k)_{i,i} = -\frac{dB_k}{dT}(1-\rho_k),\ (K_k)_i = \left[B_k(T(y_i)) - \frac{dB_k}{dT}\frac{\sum_{k^\prime}B_{k^\prime}(T_0)\kappa_{k^\prime}b_{k^\prime}}{\sum_{k^\prime}\frac{dB_{k^\prime}}{dT}\kappa_{k^\prime}b_{k^\prime}}\right](1-\rho_k)`  
  src: `haakonsen_2012_mcphac` eqs. A12-A23 (A15-A23 core); anchor: “for 1 < i < Ntemp . All other elements of Tk and Uk are zero”
- **rt.temperature-correction-spw09** [equation] — Lambda-iteration temperature correction for two modes (SPW09). The integral Lambda-iteration temperature correction at a given depth is minus the energy-balance error divided by the frequency integral of Phi_nu, built from the diagonal Lambda-operator elements of each mode and averaged opacities. The Lambda correction is used in the upper layers; the Avrett-Krook flux correction (using the relative flux error) is used in deep layers; a Kurucz surface correction is used at the surface.  
  `\Delta T_\Lambda = \frac{-\varepsilon_\Lambda(m)}{\int_0^\infty\Phi_\nu\,d\nu}, \quad \Phi_\nu = \sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[(\Lambda^i_{\nu{\rm diag}}-1)/(1-\alpha_\nu^i\Lambda^i_{\nu{\rm diag}})\right]\overline{k}_\nu^i\,(dB_\nu/dT), \quad \varepsilon_\Lambda(m) = \sum_{i=1}^{2}\int_0^\infty d\nu\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi\int_{-1}^{+1}\left((k_\nu^i+\sigma_\nu^i)I_\nu^i-\eta_\nu^i\right)d\mu, \quad \overline{k}_\nu^i = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi\int_{-1}^{+1}k_\nu^i\,d\mu`  
  src: `suleimanov_potekhin_werner_2009_mag_atm` eqs. 21-25; anchor: “modified for the two-mode radiation transfer, based on the en-”
- **rt.two-mode-transfer-spw09** [equation] — Radiative transfer equations for the two modes with scattering (SPW09). Transfer equation for the specific intensity in mode i (i = 1,2) as a function of mu and phi, with source function containing thermal emission and scattering from both modes, the optical depth defined with true absorption plus scattering opacity, and the scattering opacity obtained by integrating the differential scattering over all directions and both modes. The emissivity combines scattering and thermal terms.  
  `\mu\frac{dI_\nu^i}{d\tau_\nu^i} = I_\nu^i - S_\nu^i, \quad S_\nu^i = \frac{k_\nu^i}{k_\nu^i+\sigma_\nu^i}\frac{B_\nu}{2} + \frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{1}{k_\nu^i+\sigma_\nu^i}\sum_{j=1}^{2}\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi^\prime\int_{-1}^{+1}\sigma_\nu^{ij}(\mu,\varphi;\mu^\prime,\varphi^\prime)I_\nu^j(\mu^\prime,\varphi^\prime)d\mu^\prime, \quad d\tau_\nu^i = (k_\nu^i+\sigma_\nu^i)dm, \quad \sigma_\nu^i(\mu,\varphi) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{j=1}^{2}\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi^\prime\int_{-1}^{+1}\sigma_\nu^{ij}(\mu,\varphi;\mu^\prime,\varphi^\prime)d\mu^\prime, \quad \eta_\nu^i(\mu,\varphi) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{j=1}^{2}\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi^\prime\int_{-1}^{+1}\sigma_\nu^{ij}I_\nu^j(\mu^\prime,\varphi^\prime)d\mu^\prime + k_\nu^i\frac{B_\nu}{2}`  
  src: `suleimanov_potekhin_werner_2009_mag_atm` eqs. 5-8, 10; anchor: “2. The radiation transfer equations for the two modes”
- **rt.two-mode-transfer-val** [equation] — Mode transfer equation in Thomson optical depth (VAL06). Plane-parallel, fully ionised atmosphere with B along the normal: coupled transfer equations for the two photon modes in Thomson optical depth, with total opacity (free-free plus scattering) in units of the Thomson opacity; hydrostatic equilibrium in the same variable.  
  `\pm\mu\frac{\partial I_\nu^j(\tau,\pm\mu)}{\partial\tau} = \frac{\kappa_j^{\rm tot}}{\kappa_T}\left[I_\nu^j(\tau,\pm\mu)-S_\nu^j(\tau,\pm\mu)\right], \quad P = \frac{g}{\kappa_T}\tau, \quad d\tau = -\rho\kappa_T\,dz`  
  src: `van_adelsberg_lai_2006_magnetic_atm` eqs. 6-7; anchor: “The standard method used in all previous work involves solving the coupled radia”
- **rt.vacuum-relevance-val** [approximation] — Field strength above which vacuum resonance matters (VAL06). For B above about B_l the vacuum resonance density lies between the X-mode and O-mode photospheres for typical photon energies, so mode conversion suppresses spectral features and softens the hard X-ray tail. For B below about B_l the resonance lies outside both photospheres and the emission spectrum is unaltered, although observed polarisation is still affected.  
  `B \gtrsim B_l \simeq 6.6\times10^{13}\,T_6^{-1/8}E_1^{-1/4}S^{-1/4}\ \mathrm{G}`  
  src: `van_adelsberg_lai_2006_magnetic_atm` eq. 5; anchor: “the vacuum resonance density lies between the X-mode and O-mode photospheres”

## surface

- **surface.field-colatitude-from-geometry** [pipeline] — Magnetic colatitude of a surface point from obliquity and rotation phase. Project convention: the magnetic colatitude chi = theta_B of a surface point is the angle between the outward normal of that point and the magnetic axis. With the rotation axis as z, the magnetic axis at colatitude Psi_pole from the rotation axis and azimuth phi_rot (the rotation phase), and the surface point at colatitude theta_surf and azimuth phi_surf, the spherical law of cosines gives cos theta_B = cos Psi_pole cos theta_surf + sin Psi_pole sin theta_surf cos(phi_surf - phi_rot). For the geometric sub-observer surface point (the sub-observer point, theta_surf = theta_los, phi_surf = 0 by choice of azimuth origin) this is cos theta_B = cos i cos alpha_B + sin i sin alpha_B cos phi_rot with i = theta_los the inclination of the line of sight to the rotation axis and alpha_B = Psi_pole the magnetic obliquity.  
  `\cos\theta_B=\cos\Psi_{pole}\cos\theta_{surf}+\sin\Psi_{pole}\sin\theta_{surf}\cos(\phi_{surf}-\phi_{rot});\quad \text{sub-observer point: }\cos\chi=\cos i\cos\alpha_B+\sin i\sin\alpha_B\cos\phi_{rot}`  
  src: `PRD` Scope, In; anchor: “surface temperature and field maps constrained by the observed pulse”
- **surface.gh83-approx-1d-anisotropic-slab** [approximation] — GH83 one-dimensional anisotropic-conduction slab. Heat conduction from an isothermal reservoir (temperature T_0, depth L) to a plane surface is treated as one-dimensional with field lines threading the slab at angle Phi to the horizontal; the conductivity tensor is diagonal along/across B, flux balances sigma T^4 at the surface, dT/dx is neglected against dT/dz (R >> L), dT/dz is taken constant over the star and the temperature dependence of K is ignored.  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` Sect. II b, pp. 284-285; anchor: “is beyond the scope of this paper. By equation (12) it is to order of magnitude”
- **surface.gh83-approx-blackbody-emission** [approximation] — GH83 pure-blackbody surface emission. Citing emissivity studies (Itoh 1975, Brinkman 1980, Cheng and Helfand 1983), the authors state that both the total luminosity and spectrum should not deviate grossly from the blackbody, and assume a pure blackbody form for the surface emission in all subsequent light-curve and spectrum calculations.  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` Sect. III, p. 285; anchor: “and in the following discussion we will assume a pure blackbody form.”
- **surface.gh83-conduction-limits** [result] — Limits of the GH83 temperature distribution. For isotropic conduction (K_perp = K_par) the temperature is constant over the star. As K_perp is reduced relative to K_par the equatorial regions cool, reaching absolute zero in this approximation for K_perp/K_par = 0; the authors note a significantly cooler magnetic equator is spread over a significant fraction of the stellar surface area.  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` after eq. 15 / Fig. 2, p. 285; anchor: “In the case of isotropic conduction”
- **surface.gh83-conductivity-tensor** [equation] — Conductivity tensor in the horizontal frame (GH83 eq. 8). Rotating the diagonal tensor diag(K_par, K_perp) through the field inclination angle Phi gives the conductivity components in the horizontal (x) / vertical (z) frame.  
  `K_{11}=K_\parallel\cos^2\Phi+K_\perp\sin^2\Phi,\quad K_{12}=K_{21}=(K_\parallel-K_\perp)\cos\Phi\sin\Phi,\quad K_{22}=K_\parallel\sin^2\Phi+K_\perp\cos^2\Phi`  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` eq. 8, p. 285; anchor: “and we obtain the conductivity in the unprimed system:”
- **surface.gh83-dipole-field-inclination** [equation] — Dipole field inclination versus magnetic colatitude (GH83 eq. 15). For a purely dipolar field the angle Phi between the field lines and the local horizontal satisfies tan Phi = 2 cot beta, where beta is the magnetic colatitude.  
  `\tan\Phi = 2\cot\beta`  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` eq. 15, p. 285; anchor: “is the magnetic colatitude.”
- **surface.gh83-flux-balance** [equation] — Surface flux balance (GH83 eq. 11). The heat flux arriving at the surface from below is balanced by blackbody emission from the surface.  
  `q_z({\rm surface}) = \sigma T^4`  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` eq. 11, p. 285; anchor: “The boundary condition is that the flux arriving at the surface from below is ba”
- **surface.gh83-isotropic-density** [equation] — Density above which conduction is isotropic (GH83 eqs. 4-5). Conductivity becomes isotropic and temperature constant on horizontal surfaces once the one-dimensional electron Fermi energy greatly exceeds the cyclotron energy, rho >> 1e4 B_12^{3/2} g cm^-3, or once the Fermi energy exceeds the ionisation potential of the last atomic electron, rho >> 1.3e3 g cm^-3; both hold at very shallow depths.  
  `\rho \gg 10^4 B_{12}^{3/2}\ {\rm g\,cm^{-3}}\ (4);\qquad \rho \gg 1.3\times10^{3}\ {\rm g\,cm^{-3}}\ (5)`  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` eqs. 4-5, p. 284; anchor: “condition obtains for densities”
- **surface.gh83-pole-geometry-angle** [equation] — Pole-to-line-of-sight angle versus rotation phase (GH83 eq. 21). For a magnetic pole at geographic colatitude Psi and an observer at colatitude theta, the cosine of the angle alpha between the pole normal and the line of sight varies with pulsar phase phi as given; a similar term is centred on the other pole.  
  `\cos\alpha(t) = \cos\theta\cos\Psi + \sin\theta\sin\Psi\cos\phi`  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` eq. 21, p. 286; anchor: “magnetic poles is at geographic colatitude”
- **surface.gh83-spectrum-conclusion** [result] — GH83 conclusion on blackbody character of the observed spectrum. Within GH83's locally blackbody models filtered through the ISM and Einstein IPC, fitted spectra are approximately blackbody: unless magnetospheric heating of the polar cap is fortuitously adjusted to balance that from the remainder of the star, the observed spectrum of a star with a non-uniform temperature distribution is blackbody in nature, and the best-fit temperature closely approximates that of the polar cap.  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` Sect. III c, p. 290; anchor: “We conclude that, unless magnetospheric heating of the polar cap is fortuitously”
- **surface.gh83-surface-flux-relation** [equation] — Surface temperature from the anisotropic slab (GH83 eq. 13). With dT/dx neglected and K_22 ~ K_21, the surface temperature is related to the vertical temperature gradient and the conductivities along and across B, all evaluated at the surface.  
  `\sigma T^4 = -\left(K_\parallel\sin^2\Phi + K_\perp\cos^2\Phi\right)\frac{\partial T}{\partial z}`  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` eq. 13, p. 285; anchor: “where all quantities are evaluated at the surface.”
- **surface.gh83-synthetic-spectrum-fit** [datum] — Best-fit blackbody temperature of a synthesised GH83 spectrum. For the anisotropic-heating temperature distribution (eqs. 14-15) with T_pole = 1e6 K, K_perp/K_par = 0 and an orthogonal rotator (theta = Psi = 90 deg), N_H = 1e21 cm^-2, a blackbody fitted to the synthesised, rotation-averaged IPC spectrum has temperature 0.93e6 K with residuals below 10 percent over the spectral peak. Frozen at the pole-on phase T_fit = 0.95e6 K (residuals a few percent); at light-curve minimum (edge-on, looking at the magnetic equator) T_fit = 0.90e6 K.  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` Sect. III c, pp. 289-290; anchor: “The best-fit temperature was 0.93”
- **surface.gh83-temperature-distribution** [equation] — Greenstein-Hartke surface temperature distribution (GH83 eq. 14). With dT/dz taken constant and K independent of T, the fourth power of the surface temperature is T_pole^4 times the sum of sin^2 Phi and (K_perp/K_par) cos^2 Phi, where Phi is the angle of the field lines to the horizontal and T_pole is the polar-cap temperature.  
  `T^4 = T_{\rm pole}^4\left(\sin^2\Phi + \frac{K_\perp}{K_\parallel}\cos^2\Phi\right)`  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` eq. 14, p. 285; anchor: “where Tpole is the temperature at the polar cap and”
- **surface.notation-conduction** [notation] — Heat-conduction and polar-cap symbols (GH83). Symbols of the anisotropic heat-conduction model and the polar-cap/light-curve discussion of Greenstein and Hartke.  
  src: `greenstein_hartke_1983_surface_T` eqs. 1-3, 6-11, 23; Sect. III c, pp. 289-290; anchor: “We assume the thermal conductivity tensor to be diagonal in the primed system:”
- **surface.notation-geometry** [notation] — Surface/viewing geometry symbols (GH83, PPP15, PHC16). Angles used for magnetic colatitude, field inclination, and the pole/line-of-sight geometry. Note the sources reuse the letter theta for different angles; the project symbols here are disambiguated.
